blocks.h2: A2 · The application today, in one picture

boxes.title: Supabase (EU region)
lines: Daily backups on Pro plan only

blocks.p: What is built: a tablet-first AAC app for French, English and Arabic (eight kinds of Arabic), one code base for iPad, Android and the web; accounts and teams with roles and parental approval; a professional workspace with verification; consent-based follow-up; a back office; 24,128 pictograms from ten libraries that allow commercial use; about 49,000 lines of code with 300 unit tests, 176 database security checks and 204 accessibility scans. What is not built yet: billing, the native store apps (never built or tested on a device), copying photos and recordings between devices, switch scanning and eye gaze, two-step sign-in for the team, legal documents (privacy policy, terms).

blocks.small: Native apps only (decided 18 November 2026). The web app will not be offered to families or therapists: no web sign-in, no web demo. Its weak points (it needs internet to start; some computer voices are online) disappear. What so far only worked or was only tested in a browser must work in the native apps before launch: speech recognition (a native module: test on a real build, not Expo Go), search by drawing (written for the website; tablets still have to send the drawing as a picture) and the accessibility checks (run on the web build; VoiceOver and TalkBack still to try on devices). Therapists work on a tablet or phone, not a computer. The team's back office stays reachable inside the app (same code). The child lock works best with the device's own tools (Guided Access on iPad, screen pinning on Android). Every release now waits for store review, about 1 to 3 days, instead of a few minutes for the website. All of this is in the launch plan (next chapter).

blocks.h2: A3 · Twelve things to know

numbered: The child can always speak. The board runs from a copy on the device, works without internet, and core word positions never move. This is the right foundation for AAC.
Servers are cheap; people are not. About US$40 a month up to ~1,000 active children; 1–4 US cents per active child per month beyond. Maintenance, support and compliance are the real costs (table A4).

One habit drove scale costs: fixed. Every open board used to download the whole profile every 30 seconds. Since 17 November 2026 it asks only the version number and downloads the profile only when it changed: about 99% less traffic; servers for 100,000 children fall from about $2,860 to $875 a month.
No backups on the free plan. Move to Supabase Pro (daily backups) before real families, add a weekly off-site copy, and test a restore every quarter.
Photos and recordings live on one device. A lost tablet loses them. The private server folder exists; copying files is the next step (5–10 days). This is the main data-loss risk.

Medical device: the biggest regulatory fork. EU law covers software that "compensates for a disability". The app is likely a class I medical device unless its purpose and claims are framed otherwise; progress analytics can push it higher. Get a written opinion before marketing (section 5).

Treat the child's profile as health data. Explicit parental consent, a DPIA, probably a DPO, provider contracts; in France, possibly certified health-data hosting (HDS). The technical privacy design is already strong (section 6).
Legal documents are missing. No privacy policy or terms in the app yet: required by law and by both stores.

Billing is the plan's main missing piece. The plan (18 November 2026): App Store and Google Play only; families subscribe monthly or yearly, therapists pay once. To build: the in-app purchases, a server-side entitlement that unlocks every device of the family, "Restore purchases" and a purchase screen behind the caregiver code. The stores keep 15% and handle VAT. Write "communication is never blocked by payment" into the terms and the code (sections 12, 15).

Continuity rests on one person. Code and accounts look personal; one person maintains everything with an AI assistant. Move accounts to the company, name a backup developer, keep the good documentation up to date (section 14).
Accessibility: strong on the web, gaps for AAC access methods. 0 failures in automatic WCAG 2.2 AA scans, but no switch scanning or eye gaze, and no real screen-reader or tablet test yet (section 8).
Content needs native validation. The Arabic dialect lists and Arabic menus were written without native reviewers; automatic pictogram translations are flagged "to review" (sections 8, 20).

blocks.small: Why each line is or is not needed. Supabase Pro: backups (the free plan keeps none). Bigger server, transfer, sign-in accounts, disk: they only cost something once use grows; buy a bigger server only when measurements show the database is slow. Point-in-time recovery: Pro already keeps a daily backup for 7 days; this shrinks the worst loss from about a day to minutes. Off-site copy: advised, and cheap. E-mail service: needed once families are many (Gmail limits sending and lands in spam; free tiers cover the first few thousand e-mails a month). Apple program: required by the plan ($99 a year; Google Play's $25 once is in table A5). Domain: yes in practice: the e-mail service needs a domain you own to send from (SPF and DKIM records), and the privacy pages and store listings should carry it. Expo: needed in some form for store builds and updates (the free plan at first, the paid plan once releases are frequent, or builds on a Mac); its $19 is added when the free plan's builds are not enough. Privacy and support pages: needed, $0. The web app itself is not offered (native apps only), but both stores require a privacy-policy address, Apple a support address and Google Play a web link to ask for an account's deletion: a few static pages on Cloudflare's free plan, or any free host.

Not in the totals. (1) The AI helper is optional and switched off today (the caa-ai function is not deployed, so the app shows no AI button). If switched on, at 3 requests per active child per month: with Claude Opus 5.5 (as coded today, about $0.06 a request) add $18 / $180 / $1,800 / $9,000 / $18,000; Claude Haiku 5.5's list price is about 40 times lower ($0.10 / $0.50 against $4 / $20 per million tokens): add $1 / $6 / $60 / $300 / $600; Sonnet 5.5 costs half of Opus. Quality must be tested before changing model, Arabic first. (2) Transfer is now about 6 MB per active child per month (a version check every 30 s, a full download only after a change). (3) The stores' fee is a cost of the plan: Apple 15% under its Small Business Program (proceeds under $1M a year; you must enrol), otherwise 30%, with auto-renewing subscriptions dropping to 15% after a subscriber's first paid year; Google Play 15% on subscriptions from day one and 15% on the first $1M a year of other sales (the therapists' purchase); EU: Apple's new terms from 1 October 2026 (9.4). At the report's example prices (France, VAT included): €1.25 a month per €9.99 monthly subscription, €10.00 a year per €79.99 yearly one, and 15% of the price without VAT for the therapists' purchase, whose price is not set (table A6). The stores collect VAT, so store prices include it. Support and maintenance (sections 16 and 14) are business needs, not legal duties. In compliance (table A5): the GDPR documents (privacy notice, terms, records of processing) and very likely an impact assessment (DPIA) are legal duties for children's data; a data protection officer may be required if the data counts as health data processed at large scale (an external part-time one is usual); the accountant follows from keeping a company's books; insurance is advised rather than required. Fixed business costs (accountant, insurance, DPO): €450–1,650 a month.

The therapists' one-time price, and whether they must be verified before they can buy (0.5).
The audience declared to the stores: children included or not (0.6).
Medical device or not, after the regulatory opinion (0.7).
AI helper on or off at launch (0.9).
Who maintains the app and who is the backup (section 14).

Legal and content side by side: privacy policy and terms, DPIA, regulatory opinion, vocabulary review (P0 of table A7: 4–8 weeks)

If you build it yourself, the app work costs no developer fees; its length depends on your sessions, which the report cannot measure. ★ Critical path: seller decision → D-U-N-S (company) → store accounts, agreements, bank and tax → bundle identifier and the first EAS build → in-app billing with the server entitlement and its database migration → in-app products in both consoles → closed test (14 days for a new personal Google account) → review. Two developers shorten the app work; the 14-day test and the legal documents then set the pace. Photo sync (2.16), if included, adds 7–15 developer days.

chapters.title: Part B · Answers, question by question

blocks.p: Each section starts with a short summary, then answers every question of the questionnaire in its original order and wording. The number before each question (for example 2.7) is used for cross-references.

sections.title: Development and operating costs
sections.in_short: Running the servers is cheap: about US$40 a month up to roughly 1,000 active children, and about 1–4 US cents per active child per month after that. The real costs are people (maintenance, support), compliance (legal, audits, possibly CE marking) and, if it is switched on, the AI helper. Not all of it is obligatory. Under the plan set on 18 November 2026 (sold only in the App Store and Google Play: families subscribe monthly or yearly, therapists pay once), the minimum is about $35 a month up to 1,000 active children and about $60 at 10,000; point-in-time recovery and the off-site copy are choices (column "Needed?" of table A4). The stores' 15% on each sale is a cost of the plan (table A6). The development work the plan needs (native builds, in-app billing) costs €14,000–€34,000 only if you hire a developer; built yourself in AI-assisted sessions, as everything so far, it costs your time plus Apple's US$99 a year and Google Play's US$25 once (answer 1.1, table A5).

questions.q: What is the total cost of developing and launching the application?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: What exists today was built in AI-assisted development sessions directed by the owner (the repository's branches are Claude Code sessions). I cannot see what was paid for the AI tool or how many hours the owner spent, so the cash spent so far is: the AI tool, the owner's time, and free plans of Supabase, Cloudflare and Gmail.

To put a value on it: the code base is about 49,000 lines (42,000 lines of app TypeScript, 5,000 of database SQL and server functions, 1,700 of build scripts), 12 database migration files, 300 unit tests, 176 database security checks, an accessibility test suite and a library of 24,128 pictograms. An agency would typically quote 12–24 person-months for this scope, about €120,000–€350,000 at EU rates. This is not money to pay: it is what an agency would charge to rebuild what exists. Still to pay before a paid launch (Part A, table A5): €48,000–€147,000 if you hire a developer for the development work, or about €28,000–€101,000 in cash if you build it yourself, as you built the app so far. (This corrects the earlier figure of €25,000–€90,000, which did not add up from the table's rows.) Under the plan (App Store and Google Play only), it splits three ways:

bullets: Required by law (outside professionals, cash either way): the legal documents (privacy notice, terms) and the impact assessment (DPIA): about €7,000–€25,000.

The WORK is required by the plan, not the payment: native builds and store set-up, in-app billing with the server-side entitlement, Sign in with Apple (prepared in the app) and the stores' privacy forms (table A5b). If you hire a developer: €14,000–€34,000 (native builds €8,000–€20,000 and in-app billing €6,000–€14,000, i.e. 25–50 developer days). If you build it yourself: cash only Apple's US$99 a year and Google Play's US$25 once; test devices only if you do not already own an iPad or iPhone and an Android device (a used Android tablet is enough; no Mac is needed, since builds run in Expo's cloud); Expo's free plan at first; RevenueCat free until US$2,500 of monthly tracked revenue. Your time: several weeks of sessions instead of developer days.

Advised (outside professionals, cash either way): audits (security €6,000–€20,000, accessibility €5,000–€20,000), insurance (€1,500–€6,000) and content review (€3,000–€10,000: the French and Arabic words of the icon libraries are still marked "to review" in the app).

The other lines of table A5 follow the choices described there: company set-up and the medical-device opinion and trademark (cash either way); two-step sign-in and staging, photo sync (development work: €0 cash if you build them yourself).

answer.p: CE marking is not automatic: EU medical-device rules cover software meant to compensate for a disability, which can include AAC, so it depends on how the app's purpose is described. Ask a regulatory specialist before spending €25,000–€80,000.

questions.cost: Launch: €48k–€147k hired, ≈ €28k–€101k cash built yourself (+€25k–€80k with CE marking)
questions.source: git history; line counts; table A5

questions.q: What are the fixed monthly and annual operating costs?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Technical (fixed, whatever the number of users): Supabase Pro US$25/month (needed for daily backups: the free plan keeps none and pauses idle projects), Apple Developer Program US$99/year, Google Play US$25 once, domain €15–40/year, e-mail sending service €0–20/month, Expo build service €0–19/month, off-site backup storage about €5/month. Total about US$40–80 a month.
Business (fixed): accountant €100–300/month, insurance €125–500/month, external DPO or legal retainer €200–800/month, bank and tools €20–50/month: about €450–1,650 a month.
Together: roughly €6,000–€20,000 a year before any salary, contractor or marketing.

questions.q: What are the variable costs associated with the number of users?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: In order of size, as the app is built today:

bullets: Checking for other people's changes. Until 17 November 2026 an open board downloaded the child's whole profile every 30 seconds; that was by far the largest variable cost. Fixed on 17 November 2026: it now asks only the version number (a few hundred bytes) and downloads the profile only when someone saved a newer one, about 99% less data. It still makes one small request every 30 seconds per open board, which uses some server capacity.
AI helper, if switched on: about US$0.06 per request with the current model (Claude Opus 5.5), about US$0.002 with Claude Haiku 5.5.
Sign-in accounts above 100,000 per month: US$0.00325 each (parents, professionals and linked tablets each count).
E-mails (sign-in codes, password resets).
Database size: small (a new child profile is 12 KB).
Store fees: 15% of each sale without VAT (Apple's Small Business Program once enrolled, Google Play subscriptions), 30% outside these programs (table A6).
Support time: the largest variable cost in practice.

questions.cost: ≈ US$0.01–0.02 per active child per month (servers)

questions.q: What is the average operating cost per active user?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Servers only (Part A, table A4): about US$0.40 per active child per month at 100 children (the fixed US$40 dominates), US$0.04 at 1,000, US$0.02 at 10,000 and under US$0.01 at 50,000–100,000. (Before the fix of 17 November 2026, the last three were US$0.03–0.04.)
Add, if switched on, the AI helper: about US$0.18 per active child per month with Opus 5.5 at 3 requests a month (US$0.006 with Haiku 5.5).
All-in, with support and maintenance shared out, a realistic figure is €0.30–€1.50 per active family per month at scale. People, not servers, are the cost.

questions.q: Which external services require recurring payments?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Today, as configured in the repository: none is mandatory-paid (the docs describe free plans of Supabase, Cloudflare and a Gmail account). Once real families use the app:

bullets: Supabase Pro (monthly, plus usage) and an e-mail sending service (monthly, by volume).
Apple Developer Program (yearly) and a domain name (yearly).
Expo EAS (optional, monthly).
Anthropic API (per use, only if the AI helper is switched on).
Apple's and Google's commission on each sale (15% as a small developer) and RevenueCat (1% above US$2,500 of monthly revenue), once billing exists.
Business services: insurance, accountant, DPO.

questions.q: Which services are currently free but may become chargeable beyond certain thresholds?
questions.label: app

bullets: Supabase free plan: 500 MB database, 1 GB files, 5 GB transfer, 50,000 sign-in accounts a month; no backups; the project pauses after a week without activity. Pro includes 100,000 accounts, 8 GB database, 250 GB transfer and 100 GB files, then charges per unit.
Cloudflare: static website files are free with no request limit, but limited to 20,000 files and 25 MiB per file (the app ships 161 pictogram packs: fine).
Gmail: about 500 messages a day for a personal account; not built for an app's e-mails.
Expo EAS: a few free builds a month at low priority.
RevenueCat: free up to US$2,500 of monthly tracked revenue, then 1%.
Google sign-in: free. Apple sign-in: needs the paid Apple program.
SMS sign-in (Twilio or similar): paid per message from the first one (switched off today).

questions.source: supabase.com/pricing; Cloudflare static assets limits; expo.dev/pricing

questions.q: Are there hidden or indirect costs that we should anticipate?
questions.label: estimate

bullets: Store commission (15–30%) and VAT taken before you are paid.
Currency: the stores pay you in your account's currency at their own rates; nothing to pay on top.
Two or three framework upgrades a year (Expo / React Native) and yearly iOS / Android changes: 2–5 developer days each.
Test devices (an iPad, two Android tablets, a phone): €1,500–3,000.
Native-speaker review of each Arabic dialect list and of the Arabic menus: €3,000–10,000.
Translating legal documents for each new country.
Professionals' verification is manual work in the back office (10–20 minutes each).
Yearly security and accessibility re-tests.
Moving the founder's personal accounts (GitHub, Gmail, Supabase, Cloudflare) to company accounts.
Possibly a more expensive host if French health-data hosting rules (HDS) apply (section 6).
The AI helper if it is offered without limits.

questions.cost: Budget 10–20% on top of visible costs

questions.q: What is the estimated annual maintenance budget?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Rule of thumb: 15–25% of the build value per year, i.e. €20,000–€70,000.

A lean but safe budget: a developer 3–5 days a month (€15,000–€35,000 a year as a freelancer), yearly security and accessibility re-tests (€5,000–€15,000), servers and tools (€1,000–€5,000 up to about 10,000 children), legal updates (€2,000–€8,000): about €25,000–€60,000 a year.
If the founder keeps doing the development with an AI assistant, the cash part drops to €8,000–€25,000, but the dependence on one person stays (section 14).

questions.q: What are the costs associated with developing and releasing new features?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: From this project's own history: a small feature (the "Back" button, the "?" help beside each set-up question) takes 1–3 developer days; a medium one ("Keep me logged in", e-mails to the team) 3–8 days; a large one (the back office product pages, a professional handing a profile to parents) 10–25 days. At €450–650 a day for a freelancer: €500–€15,000 per feature.

Every user-visible feature also costs: the guide in three languages, tests, the accessibility scan, store review for the native apps (1–3 days), and, if the app becomes a medical device, a change record and risk review.

questions.q: What are the operating costs for 100, 1,000, 10,000, 50,000 and 100,000 active users?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Servers and services per month (US$), counting an active user as an active child's board (about 2.5 sign-in accounts each). Details in Part A, table A4, and Appendix B.

bullets: 10,000: about $185 (it was about $400 before the fix of 17 November 2026).

answer.p: Most of the remaining cost at 100,000 is sign-in accounts above 100,000 a month ($488).
If the AI helper is switched on with Opus 5.5 (3 requests per child per month): add $18, $180, $1,800, $9,000, $18,000. With Haiku 5.5: add $1, $6, $60, $300, $600.
Not included: the stores' 15% on each sale (table A6), support staff, maintenance, compliance.

sections.title: Hosting, storage and infrastructure
sections.in_short: The database, sign-in, private files and two small server functions are on Supabase. Under the plan (native apps only, decided 18 November 2026) Cloudflare only serves the privacy and support pages the stores require; the web app is not offered. The child's board lives on each device and works without internet; the server keeps the shared copy. Pictograms ship inside the app, so they cost nothing per user. Photos and recordings stay on the device that made them: that is the main gap.

questions.q: Where will the application and its database be hosted?
questions.label: app

bullets: Database, sign-in, private files, server functions: Supabase (managed PostgreSQL). The set-up guide says to create the project in a European region (Frankfurt or Paris). Confirm the real region in Supabase → Project Settings → General: it cannot be changed later without a migration.

Static pages: Cloudflare (free). Today it serves the web app; under the plan (native apps only) only the privacy-policy, support and account-deletion pages the stores require. It stores no data and holds no secret.
Native apps: Apple App Store and Google Play (not built yet).
E-mails (sign-in codes, team messages): a Gmail account through SMTP.

questions.q: Which hosting providers are being used and why?
questions.label: app

bullets: Supabase: one service gives PostgreSQL with row-level security (the database itself decides who sees each row), sign-in, private file storage and server functions. It is open source, so it can be self-hosted or replaced, and it offers EU regions.
Cloudflare: free, unlimited delivery of static files, automatic rebuild from GitHub, and the browser protections in public/_headers; under the plan it only carries the privacy and support pages.
Gmail: the quickest way to send sign-in codes. To replace before scale (deliverability, daily limits, and a data-processing agreement).
Expo EAS (planned): builds the iPad app in the cloud without a Mac.

questions.q: Which data is stored locally on the user's device and which data is stored in the cloud?
questions.label: app

answer.p: On the device: the copy of the child's board (so it works offline), photos, recorded voices, the built-in words and the 24,128 pictograms (inside the native app), the follow-up days (120 days, only if the family turned it on), counters waiting to be sent (only with consent), the session (unless "Keep me logged in" is unticked).

In the cloud (Supabase): accounts, child profiles (the board as one document plus a version number), team members and rights, invitations, proposals, change history (never what the child said), devices, follow-up days (only with consent), adults' observations, professionals' verification files (the identity document is deleted after the decision), notices, materials, messages to the team, votes, consent-based counters, technical-problem counts, AI call counts, the team's action log.
Nowhere by default: the sentences the child says (only at the highest follow-up level chosen by the family).

questions.q: How much storage is required per user?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Measured: a new child profile is 12 KB (2.7 KB compressed). A well-customised profile is probably 30–150 KB. The change history adds about 0.5–1 KB per change; follow-up days, if turned on, 2–10 KB per day and device.

Estimate: about 0.2 MB at the start, plus 0.2–0.5 MB a year per child. 100,000 children: roughly 20–70 GB of database. Photos and recordings: nothing in the cloud today; if they are synced later, expect 5–30 MB per child.

questions.q: Does storage capacity need to increase as the number of users increases?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, slowly. On Supabase Pro the database disk grows by itself (8 GB included, then US$0.125 per GB a month). Storage only becomes a noticeable cost once photos and recordings are synced; even then, 100,000 children × 20 MB = 2 TB costs about US$42 a month.

questions.q: What is the cost of additional storage?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Database: about US$0.125 per GB per month beyond 8 GB. Files: about US$0.021 per GB per month beyond 100 GB. Off-site backup copies: €0.005–0.02 per GB per month at most object-storage providers. Prices from Supabase's public list (November 2026): re-check before budgeting.

questions.q: Are there additional costs for data transfers, downloads and server requests?
questions.label: app

bullets: Supabase: data leaving the database is billed beyond 250 GB a month on Pro (about US$0.09 per GB). Requests are not billed one by one, but they use the server's capacity (compute).

The app: until 17 November 2026 it re-downloaded the whole profile every 30 seconds while a board was open (estimated 130–650 MB per active child per month). Fixed: it now asks only the version number and downloads the profile only when it changed: about 6 MB per active child per month, so 250 GB covers about 40,000 active children.
Cloudflare: website and pictogram downloads are free.
Stores: app downloads are free for you.

questions.q: Are standard pictograms and resources stored once or duplicated for each user?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Once. They ship inside the native app, and a child's profile only stores a reference such as mulberry/apple, never the picture. The built-in words are also references. So the 59 MB pictogram library costs nothing per user.

questions.q: How are personalized photos, recordings, videos and communication boards stored?
questions.label: app

bullets: Boards, words, settings, schedules: one document per child in the database, copied on each device, synced and merged.

Photos and recordings: only on the device that made them. A private storage folder for them exists on the server (profile-media) but copying files is not built. A lost tablet loses its photos and recordings; a parent's photo does not appear on the child's tablet.
Videos: not supported.

answer.p: Recommendation: build media sync before the paid launch (compressed photos about 200 KB, recordings already trimmed of silence, about 30 KB).

questions.q: How much storage is allocated to each user?
questions.label: app

answer.p: No quota today, except professionals' verification files (20 files of 10 MB at most). When photo sync exists, set a generous fair-use limit per child (for example 500 photos and 1,000 recordings, about 150 MB) so that one account cannot fill the storage.

questions.q: Should different subscription plans include different storage limits?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: My advice: no limit on anything the child needs to communicate (words, boards, photos of their people and places, recordings). The app already promises that "the child will always be able to communicate"; storage is cheap. Make plans differ by adult tools instead: professional workspace, several children, follow-up analytics, AI suggestions, materials sharing. Keep one high fair-use cap for everyone.

questions.q: How are inactive accounts and their associated storage managed?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Nothing automatic today, except: invitations expire after 30 days, rate-limit logs after 2 days, consent-based counters after 180 days, identity documents at the decision.

Proposed rule (to confirm with the lawyer): after 24 months without any sign-in, e-mail a warning, then delete 60 days later, after offering an export; never delete a child's profile without warning; keep invoices 10 years (France). Storage cost is not the reason; the GDPR requires not keeping data longer than needed.

questions.q: What are the costs associated with backups and data recovery?
questions.label: app

bullets: Free plan: no backups at all.
Pro (US$25): daily backups kept 7 days, included.
Point-in-time recovery (restore to any minute): an add-on from about US$100 a month; worth it from about 10,000 active children.
Your own weekly encrypted copy to another provider (so that losing the Supabase account is not fatal): about €5 a month plus half a day to set up.
A restore test every quarter: half a day.

answer.p: The devices also keep the latest board, which limits real losses.

questions.q: Can we change hosting providers without disrupting the application?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, with planning. The database is standard PostgreSQL and every rule is in SQL files in the repository; Supabase itself is open source and can run on another host (for example an HDS-certified host in France). The static pages are plain files that any host can serve. The app talks to the server through one interface (src/backend/Backend.ts).
Effort: 5–15 developer days plus a short maintenance window; sign-ins would need to be renewed.
Supabase-specific parts to re-create: sign-in, file storage, the two server functions, the scheduled weekly e-mail (pg_cron, pg_net). Devices keep working offline during the move.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

sections.title: Scalability and performance
sections.in_short: The design scales well because the child's board runs on the device. One background habit (download the whole profile every 30 seconds) limited scale and drove cost; it was fixed on 17 November 2026 (only a version number travels now). Server size is chosen by hand on Supabase, not automatic, and nothing has been load-tested yet.

questions.q: How many users can the current infrastructure support?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Estimate, to be confirmed by a load test: on the smallest server (Micro), a few thousand active children, i.e. about 1,000 boards open at the same moment, with the old 30-second download; since the fix each check is one tiny query, so a Medium server should serve 50,000 or more active children. The included 100,000 sign-in accounts a month is reached at about 40,000 active children.

questions.q: How many simultaneous users can the application support?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: The number that matters is boards open at the same moment, because each one asks the server every 30 seconds. Rough capacity before the 17 November fix: Micro about 1,000; Small about 2,000; Medium 5,000–8,000; Large about 15,000. Now that each check returns a single number, several times more (a load test should confirm it). Speaking itself never depends on the server.

questions.q: Does the infrastructure scale automatically as the number of users increases?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Partly. Supabase's disk grows by itself and its server functions scale by themselves; Cloudflare scales by itself. The database server size (compute) does not: you choose it, and changing it means a restart of a few minutes. Boards keep working during that restart.

questions.q: At what point will additional infrastructure or development be required?
questions.label: estimate

bullets: Done (17 November 2026): the 30-second refresh only asks for a version number.
Before real families: move to Pro (backups).
Around 5,000: a bigger server, point-in-time recovery, a real e-mail service, monitoring.
Around 20,000+: on-call arrangement, a read replica if reports slow the database.
Above 100,000 sign-in accounts a month: per-account fees start.
First institutional customers: Supabase Team plan (US$599/month) for its SOC 2 report and single sign-on, if they ask.

questions.q: What are the financial implications of scaling?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Server costs grow almost in line with users and stay small (1–4 US cents per active child per month, under 1 cent after the fix). There are steps when the server is upsized (Micro → Small → Medium → Large → XL: about $10, $15, $60, $110, $210 a month) and when sign-in accounts pass 100,000.
Fixed costs (people, compliance) do not grow with users, so the margin improves with scale. The exception is the AI helper, which costs per use.

questions.q: Can sudden increases in usage affect application performance?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes for the server side: a spike (start of the school year, a post that goes viral) multiplies the 30-second checks (each one is now tiny); the database can slow down, so saving changes, signing in and linking tablets get slow. Children can still speak: the board runs from the device copy.
Protection: the lighter checks (done), a server one size larger than needed, Supabase's spending cap and alerts, and the rate limits already in the database for sensitive actions.

questions.q: Can we monitor infrastructure usage and costs in real time?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Nearly. Supabase's dashboard shows daily usage (transfer, accounts, database size) and live reports on requests, CPU and memory; Cloudflare shows traffic; the Anthropic console shows AI spending; the back office shows AI calls per day and devices by version. Costs are updated daily, not minute by minute.

questions.q: Can we configure spending limits and automatic alerts?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes. Supabase Pro has a spending cap (on by default: it stops extra billing, which can also restrict the service when a quota is reached) and billing e-mails. Anthropic lets you set a monthly limit; the app already limits AI to 40 requests per account per day plus a ceiling for the whole service. Recommended: keep the cap on until usage is understood, alerts at 50/80/100% of budget.

questions.q: Can we identify which features consume the most technical resources?
questions.label: app

answer.p: By design today: (1) the 30-second checks for others' changes: most requests, but tiny since the 17 November fix (before it, over 90% of the data transferred); (2) the upload of follow-up days and counters, once a minute per device and only with consent; (3) AI requests (money rather than load); (4) back-office queries (rare). Supabase's query performance report can confirm this with real traffic.

questions.q: How will application performance be tested under different levels of demand?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Not done yet. Proposal: a load test with a tool such as k6 against a copy of the server (never the real one): 1,000 / 5,000 / 20,000 open boards refreshing, saves and sign-ins, measuring response times and CPU. Plus device tests on a low-end Android tablet and an older iPad (board with 81 cards, folder changes, delay before the voice speaks). Cost: 3–6 developer days and a test project (about $10–25 a month while testing).

sections.title: International distribution and regulatory compliance
sections.in_short: No country requires a special licence to distribute an AAC app as such. What changes from country to country is: whether it is a medical device, how children's and health data must be handled, how subscriptions must be sold and cancelled, taxes, and language. The app's design (parents in control, no advertising, no trackers, opt-in data) is a good starting point everywhere. This section is a map for the lawyer, not legal advice.

questions.q: What are the legal requirements for distributing an AAC application in each country?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Think in seven layers, and check each per country: (1) product law: is it a medical device (section 5)? (2) privacy and children's data; (3) health data rules; (4) consumer law for digital content and subscriptions; (5) tax; (6) accessibility rules for public buyers; (7) store rules and language laws. Nothing requires an "AAC licence" in the countries listed, unless the app is a regulated medical device.

questions.q: What are the specific requirements in France, the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Lebanon, the UAE, Saudi Arabia and other Arab countries?
questions.label: expert

bullets: France / EU: GDPR (parental consent under 15 in France; 13–16 elsewhere); health data (art. 9) means explicit consent, a DPIA and probably a DPO; French health-data hosting certification (HDS, Public Health Code L.1111-8) if the data is health data collected for care or follow-up: a key question; MDR if a medical device; consumer code (14-day withdrawal, cancellation in three clicks since June 2023); French language for consumer terms; AI Act transparency for AI features (from August 2026); Cyber Resilience Act if not a medical device (reporting from September 2026, full from December 2027); new Product Liability Directive, software included, from 9 December 2026.

United Kingdom: UK GDPR, ICO registration fee, the Children's Code (Age Appropriate Design Code); MHRA registration and a UK Responsible Person if a medical device; Consumer Rights Act; the new subscription rules of the DMCC Act (reported for January 2027).

United States: COPPA for children under 13 (verifiable parental consent; amended rule in force since 2025, compliance by April 2026); state privacy laws, including health-data laws such as Washington's My Health My Data Act; HIPAA only when working for clinics that are covered entities (business associate agreement); FERPA and state student-privacy laws for schools; auto-renewal laws (California); FDA for devices.

Canada: PIPEDA; Quebec Law 25 (privacy impact assessment before sending data outside Quebec, consent under 14 by a parent); French language obligations in Quebec; provincial health-information laws for clinicians; Health Canada for devices.

Lebanon: Law 81/2018 on electronic transactions and personal data (declaration of processing to the Ministry of Economy and Trade, licence for health data); Ministry of Public Health for medical devices; consumer protection law 659/2005.

UAE: Federal Decree-Law 45/2021 on personal data; Federal Law 2/2019 on ICT in health, which requires health data to stay in the UAE in many cases; Dubai and Abu Dhabi health authority rules; medical device registration; VAT 5%.

Saudi Arabia: Personal Data Protection Law (enforced since September 2024, SDAIA), with stricter rules for health data and transfers; SFDA marketing authorisation and a local authorised representative for medical devices; Arabic for consumer information; VAT 15%.

Other Arab countries: data laws in Qatar (13/2016), Bahrain (30/2018), Oman (6/2022), Kuwait (CITRA regulation), Jordan (24/2023), Egypt (151/2020, licences for transfers), Morocco (09-08, authorisation for health data).

questions.q: Are there countries where the application cannot be distributed without prior authorization?
questions.label: expert

bullets: If it is a medical device: Saudi Arabia (SFDA authorisation before sale), the UAE, Egypt and Lebanon (registration), the EU for class IIa or higher (notified body; class I is self-declared but registered).
For data: Lebanon (declaration / licence for health data), Egypt (licences), Morocco (authorisation for health data).
Sanctions: the stores and payment providers exclude sanctioned countries; check current lists before selling in Syria (one of the app's dialects), whose sanctions changed in 2025.

answer.p: If the app is not a medical device and holds no health data, most countries need no prior authorisation.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: Do we need a local company, representative, licence or registration in certain countries?
questions.label: expert

bullets: A company outside the EU needs an EU representative for the GDPR (art. 27) and, for a medical device, an EU authorised representative; an EU company avoids both.
UK: a UK GDPR representative without a UK establishment; a UK Responsible Person for devices.
Saudi Arabia: a local authorised representative for devices; possibly a representative under the PDPL. UAE: a local representative to register a device.
Tax: non-resident VAT registrations (often simplified online) in the UK, Gulf states, Canada.
US: none for privacy; a US agent only if registering a device with the FDA.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: Are there specific regulations for applications intended for individuals with disabilities?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Rarely a law of its own. What applies: medical device law (its definition includes "compensation for a disability"), accessibility laws (mostly for public bodies and some services), anti- discrimination law, and the conditions of public funding schemes (for example Medicare's rules for speech-generating devices in the US, or French disability compensation). The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (right to communicate, art. 21) shapes public purchasing.

questions.q: Are there specific regulations for applications used by minors?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Yes: GDPR art. 8 (parental consent, age 13–16 by country), the UK Children's Code, COPPA in the US, Quebec's rule under 14, guardian consent in Gulf laws, and the stores' children's policies (Apple Kids category, Google Play Families). The app's design is favourable: the parent creates the account and the child's profile; the child has no account; there is no advertising, no tracker, no chat with strangers and nothing public.

questions.q: Are there country-specific requirements regarding accessibility, security and privacy?
questions.label: expert

bullets: Accessibility: EU (EN 301 549, the European Accessibility Act), France (RGAA for public bodies), UK (public sector regulations), US (Section 508, ADA Title II for public schools and services), Canada (Accessible Canada Act, Ontario's AODA). Mostly binding when selling to public bodies.

Security: France (HDS for health data hosts), UAE (health data law), Saudi (national cybersecurity controls for government customers), US (HIPAA security rule for business associates), EU (Cyber Resilience Act).
Privacy: see 4.2.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: Are there restrictions regarding the international transfer of personal data?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Yes. GDPR chapter V: keeping everything in the EU region helps, but Supabase, Cloudflare, Google and Anthropic are US companies: you need their data-processing agreements, with standard contractual clauses or the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. Saudi, UAE, Egyptian and Quebec laws have their own transfer rules (assessment, safeguards or licence).

questions.q: Are there countries that require data to be stored locally?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: For health data: the UAE (Federal Law 2/2019, with exceptions) and, in practice, Saudi Arabia for health and government customers. France does not require localisation but certification of the host (HDS), which can be in the EEA. If the Gulf becomes a priority market for clinics and hospitals, plan a regional server (AWS has UAE and Bahrain regions; Supabase can be self-hosted there).

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: Must legal documents be available in the official language of each country?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: In practice yes: French is required for consumer contracts in France (Toubon law) and in Quebec; Arabic is expected or required for consumer information in Saudi Arabia and the UAE; the GDPR requires information people can understand. The app already speaks French, English and Arabic: legal documents in those three languages cover the target markets.

questions.q: What consumer protection regulations apply to digital products and subscriptions?
questions.label: expert

bullets: EU: Consumer Rights Directive (information before purchase, 14-day withdrawal, which ends when the consumer asks for immediate access and acknowledges it), Digital Content Directive (conformity and security updates), unfair terms, price-reduction rules; France: cancellation in three clicks, reminders before tacit renewal.
UK: Consumer Rights Act 2015; DMCC subscription regime (reminders, easy exit, cooling-off at renewal) reported for January 2027.
US: state automatic-renewal laws (California), ROSCA, FTC rules.
Canada: provincial laws (Quebec's is strict).
Gulf: Saudi e-commerce law, UAE consumer protection law 15/2020.

answer.p: Under the plan, the stores handle cancellation, renewal and refund requests for every sale; you still owe clear information before purchase (price, renewal, what the subscription includes) and a service that works as described.

questions.q: What are the costs associated with regulatory compliance in each country?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Without medical-device status, rough first-year legal costs: France/EU base €10,000–€30,000 (then €5,000–€15,000 a year); each further EU language €1,000–€3,000; UK +€2,000–€5,000; US +€5,000–€15,000 (more with HIPAA); Canada +€3,000–€8,000; Lebanon +€1,000–€4,000; UAE or Saudi +€5,000–€15,000 each. A medical-device route adds much more per country (section 5).

questions.q: How will we monitor changes in international regulations after launch?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: A compliance register (one line per law: applies?, owner, last checked), free newsletters of regulators (CNIL, ICO, EDPB, FTC, MHRA, SFDA, SDAIA) and law firms, Apple and Google developer news, and a yearly half-day review with the lawyer (€1,000–€3,000). Review again before each new country and before any feature that touches health claims or children's data.

sections.title: Medical device and assistive technology classification
sections.in_short: This is the biggest regulatory fork. Under the EU Medical Device Regulation, software intended to "compensate for a disability" is a medical device. An app sold to help children who cannot speak to communicate is therefore likely to be one (probably class I, self-declared), unless its intended purpose and claims are framed otherwise. Progress analytics and recommendations can push it to a higher class. Get a written qualification opinion before marketing.

questions.q: Is the application classified as a medical device, an assistive technology, educational software or a general communication tool?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: It depends on its intended purpose, as the manufacturer states it. The EU definition (MDR art. 2(1)) covers software intended for the "alleviation of, or compensation for, an injury or disability". An app presented as helping people with communication disabilities communicate is likely inside it. Several AAC products are on the EU market as class I medical devices (check competitors in the EU database EUDAMED). "Assistive technology" is a functional term, not a legal class. Presenting the app as a general communication and learning tool can be argued, but the target users (children with communication disabilities), the speech-therapist workspace and the progress follow-up make that harder.
Most likely EU reading: class I medical device software (rule 11: "all other software"), unless features push it to class IIa.

questions.source: MDR 2017/745 art. 2(1), Annex VIII rule 11; MDCG 2019-11

questions.q: Does this classification vary from one country to another?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Yes. EU: MDR. UK: UK MDR 2002 (MHRA); CE-marked devices are accepted in Great Britain for a transition period. US: FDA, where "powered communication systems" have their own classification regulation (21 CFR 890.3710) and low-risk software often benefits from enforcement discretion.

Canada: Health Canada (low-risk software is class I). Saudi Arabia: SFDA. UAE, Lebanon, Egypt: national registration. Some countries treat AAC apps as ordinary software in practice; the same claims can lead to different answers.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: Which application features could influence its regulatory classification?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Features that add risk: claims of therapy or improvement; the follow-up page (language metrics, 19 communication functions guessed by rules); adults' observations; any recommendation of goals, vocabulary level or therapy; AI suggestions presented as clinical. Features that do not: the pictogram board, speech, schedules, timers, printing. The app already describes its function recognition as "a guide for the speech therapist, not an assessment": keep that discipline.

questions.q: Does the addition of clinical assessment, progress monitoring or automated recommendations change its classification?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Yes, it can move it up. Under rule 11, software that provides information used to take decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes is class IIa or higher, which requires a notified body (an independent certifier), a certified quality system and 12–24 months. To stay in class I: keep the follow-up descriptive (counts and charts, no scores labelled as assessment, no automatic therapy recommendations), and let the professional draw conclusions.

questions.q: Do marketing claims and descriptions influence its classification?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Yes, decisively. The intended purpose is read from the labelling, the instructions, the store description, the website and promotional statements (MDR art. 2(12)). Words such as "therapy", "treatment", "clinically proven", "assessment", "improves language development" raise the risk.
Write a short claims guide (allowed and forbidden phrases in three languages) and have every store text and post checked against it.

questions.q: Do we need CE marking or other regulatory certifications?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: If it is a medical device in the EU: yes, CE marking under the MDR. For class I that is a self-declaration, but it needs real work: technical documentation, a list of the general safety and performance requirements, risk management (ISO 14971), a software life-cycle (IEC 62304), usability engineering (IEC 62366-1), a clinical evaluation, post-market surveillance, vigilance, a person responsible for regulatory compliance (PRRC), a UDI and registration in EUDAMED.

If it is not a medical device: no MDR marking, but the Cyber Resilience Act will require a CE marking for "products with digital elements" from December 2027 (self-assessment for this kind of app). Either way, some CE marking by 2027.

questions.q: Do we need to register the application with national health authorities?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: If it is a medical device: EU registration of the manufacturer and the device in EUDAMED; UK MHRA registration; FDA establishment registration and listing in the US (unless exempt); SFDA marketing authorisation in Saudi Arabia; registration in the UAE, Lebanon (Ministry of Public Health) and Egypt. If it is not, none of these.

questions.cost: UK and US registration fees: a few hundred to ~US$10k/year
questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: Are clinical studies or evidence of effectiveness required?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: For a class I device: a clinical evaluation is required, but it can usually rest on published evidence about AAC and speech-generating devices plus a post-market follow-up plan; a new clinical study is generally not needed. For funders, institutions and reimbursement, real evidence helps a lot: a pilot with speech therapists, usability studies, and the consent-based usage figures.

questions.q: Are there quality management requirements?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Yes if it is a medical device, even class I (MDR art. 10(9)): a quality management system proportionate to the risk. ISO 13485 certification is not mandatory for class I, but it is the usual way to organise it. This conflicts with today's working rule "every finished change goes straight to the live app": a medical device needs change control (record, risk review, testing, release approval) for every release.

questions.source: MDR art. 10(9); ISO 13485; CLAUDE.md publishing rule

questions.q: What are the costs of obtaining and maintaining the necessary certifications?
questions.label: estimate

bullets: Not a medical device: qualification opinion and claims guide, €3,000–€9,000 once.
EU class I: €25,000–€80,000 the first year with a consultant (quality system, technical file, clinical evaluation, external PRRC €3,000–€10,000 a year), then €10,000–€30,000 a year.
Class IIa: notified body €30,000–€100,000 initially, then €10,000–€25,000 a year, plus ISO 13485 certification.
Each extra country: €5,000–€20,000 a year (registration, representative).

questions.q: Could the application qualify for reimbursement through healthcare systems, insurance providers or disability funding programmes?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Possibly, mostly through disability or education budgets rather than health insurance:

bullets: France: disability compensation (PCH, technical aids, through the MDPH) and school adapted equipment; CE marking is often expected.
UK: NHS specialised AAC services and local commissioning (procurement frameworks).
US: Medicare and Medicaid cover speech-generating devices (codes E2500–E2599; E2511 for software on a tablet) after a speech-therapy evaluation, often through a medical equipment supplier.
Canada: provincial programmes (e.g. Ontario's Assistive Devices Program).
Gulf: government disability bodies and ministries of education (tenders); insurance rarely.
Lebanon: NGOs and international agencies.

answer.p: Generally this needs medical-device status, evidence and sometimes a dedicated-device bundle. Under the plan, families and therapists pay in the stores; funding schemes may later reimburse families.

sections.title: Privacy and data protection
sections.in_short: Privacy by design is already strong: data collection is off by default, the family alone decides, the team only sees sums over at least 5 children of 5 families, and nothing the child says is kept unless the family chooses it. What is missing is the legal paperwork (privacy policy, consent text, DPIA, records, contracts with providers) and a few rights features. A child's AAC profile should be treated as health data.

questions.q: What personal data will the application collect?
questions.label: app

bullets: Adults: e-mail, name, password (stored scrambled by Supabase), sign-in provider, menu language, preferences, devices (name, system, app version, last seen), invitations, messages to the team, votes.

Professionals, in addition: profession, country, practice details, diploma or licence and an identity document (the identity document is deleted once the check is decided), verification status, their own caregiver code.

The child: first name (can be a nickname), age, gender (for grammar and voice), languages, Arabic dialect, the board itself (words, folders, schedules, activities that can reveal daily life or health, e.g. "medicine"), the caregiver code, settings.

Only if the family turns it on: per day and device, sessions, minutes, touches, places, words used (level 2), sentences (level 3); adults' observations; anonymous usage counters and technical-problem counts (no error message).
Technical: IP addresses in Supabase and Cloudflare logs; session tokens.
On the device only: photos and recordings.

questions.q: Which data may be considered sensitive, clinical or health-related?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Using an AAC app suggests a disability, so the child's profile can reveal health information (GDPR art. 9). Most clearly health-related: the follow-up data, observations, the link "speech therapist of this child", and words on the board about health. The board can also reveal religion (prayer words) or family situation. Safest course: treat the whole child profile as special-category data.
Professionals' identity documents are not special-category but are high-risk.

questions.q: Which data is necessary for the application to function?
questions.label: app

answer.p: For the adult: an e-mail and password (or Google / Apple sign-in). For the child: the board and its settings. For sharing: team membership and devices. Not necessary: the child's real name (a nickname works), exact age (used for set-up suggestions), follow-up data, counters, AI requests.

questions.q: Which data can be collected anonymously?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Truly anonymous today: the aggregated figures the team sees (at least 5 children of 5 families, no name, word or sentence) and technical-problem counts (stored with no link to a child, account or device). The per-child counters stored on the server before they are added up are pseudonymous, i.e. still personal data (docs/SECURITY.md point 6): the "5 children" rule protects what the team sees, it is not proof of anonymity.

questions.q: Which data requires explicit user consent?
questions.label: expert

bullets: Processing the child's health-related data: explicit consent of the parent (art. 9(2)(a)), unless the lawyer finds another basis.
The follow-up recording (already opt-in, off by default, three levels).
Sharing anonymous statistics with the company (already opt-in, versioned: shareTerms).
Sending photos to the AI helper, especially photos showing people.
Marketing e-mails.
Professionals' access to a child (already: the family invites or approves).
Microphone, camera and photos (system permission).

answer.p: Creating an account itself rests on the contract.

questions.q: Can users access the application without creating an account?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Partly. "Try it first, without an account" opens a demonstration on the device; nothing is sent to the server. A tablet linked with a code uses an account without e-mail. There is no permanent "offline only, no account" mode: worth considering for privacy-minded families and as a fallback.

questions.q: How will we comply with GDPR and equivalent international privacy regulations?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Steps: (1) data map (this document, 2.3 and 6.1, is a start); (2) record of processing (art. 30); (3) legal basis per purpose; (4) DPIA; (5) privacy policy in FR/EN/AR (none in the app today); (6) consent at sign-up for the child's data; (7) procedures for access, export and deletion requests; (8) contracts with every provider (Supabase, Cloudflare, Google, Anthropic, later RevenueCat) and transfer safeguards; (9) retention schedule; (10) breach procedure; (11) a DPO. The technical side (opt-in, minimisation, row-level security) is already well ahead.

questions.source: GDPR; docs/SECURITY.md 'to confirm with a lawyer'

questions.q: Do we need a Data Protection Officer (DPO)?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Probably yes once there are many children: a DPO is mandatory when the core activity is large-scale processing of special-category data (art. 37), and children's communication data with health aspects is the core of this app. Start with an external DPO service (€200–€800 a month); it also answers families' questions.

questions.q: Do we need a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Almost certainly: health data, vulnerable people (children), potentially large scale and AI features are all on the CNIL's list of criteria. Do it before real families use the app; the CNIL offers a free PIA tool. €3,000–€10,000 with a consultant.

questions.q: How will parental consent be obtained where required?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Today the parent creates the account and the child's profile; the child never has an account; only the family can turn on follow-up or sharing (the database refuses anyone else); while a professional owns a profile, recording and sharing are locked off until the parents take it over.

To add: at sign-up, a statement that the person is the parent or legal guardian and agrees to the processing of the child's data (including health aspects), stored with the date and the text version. In the US under COPPA, "verifiable" parental consent (card check, signed form, ID check…) may be needed: lawyer's call.

questions.q: How will consent and authorization be managed for adult AAC users who require decision-making support?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Today everything is written around "the family" and "the child". For adults: let the person own the account where they can (supported decision-making), invite supporters as team members with limited rights, explain choices in easy-read form with pictograms, and let the person withdraw a supporter. Where a court appointed a guardian (e.g. tutelle or curatelle in France), that person consents within their mandate. Needs a "this board is for me" option and adult wording.

questions.q: Are the words, sentences and messages communicated by AAC users stored or accessible?
questions.label: app

answer.p: By default, no: follow-up is off, the sentence strip is not saved, and the change history never contains what the child said. If the family chooses: level "use" (counts only), "words" (which words), "sentences" (the sentences), stored per day on the server and visible to the parents, team managers and members the parents allowed to "see the progress data". Never in the team's figures.
Recommendation: a shorter retention for sentence-level data (e.g. 12 months) and field-level encryption.

questions.q: Who can access users' personal information and communication content?
questions.label: app

answer.p: The family; team members according to the rights the family gave (enforced by the database); the app's team sees only aggregated figures in the back office. Technically, anyone who can open the Supabase dashboard can read the whole database: keep that to one or two named people with two-step sign-in and a confidentiality commitment. Supabase staff only under its data-processing agreement.
Anthropic receives only a topic, photo or drawing, if the AI helper is on.

questions.q: How will access rights be managed between AAC users, parents, professionals and institutions?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Already built: roles (therapist, teacher, caregiver, family member, other), three levels (use, contribute by proposals, direct editing), individual permissions (see progress data, invite…), end dates, instant removal, professionals only after their certificate is accepted, invitations never give more than their author has, core word positions always need the parents' approval. All enforced in the database and tested by 176 checks. Institutions as such are not modelled yet (section 17).

questions.q: How long will personal data be retained?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Defined today: follow-up days on the device 120 days; counters 180 days; rate-limit logs 2 days; invitations valid 30 days; identity documents until the decision. Everything else stays until the user deletes it.

Proposed schedule (to validate): follow-up days 24 months rolling; change history 24 months; messages to the team 3 years; team action log 5 years; inactive accounts 24 months then deletion with warning; invoices 10 years.

questions.q: How can users access, modify, export or permanently delete their data?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Exists: edit in the app; export the profile as a file (Account → Privacy); export observations and follow-up as CSV; erase recorded follow-up data; delete the child's profile or the whole account after typing a confirmation word (the database deletes every linked row); signing out erases the device copies.

Missing: one "download all my data" file covering the account, teams and history; guaranteed deletion of stored files on the server (done from the app today, best effort); a published channel (privacy e-mail) and a 1-month answer process.

questions.q: How is personal data removed from backups?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: It is not removed one by one: deleted data disappears when the backups expire (7 days on Supabase Pro daily backups; 7–28 days with point-in-time recovery). That is accepted practice if documented: backups are only restored after a disaster, and then the deletions are applied again from a list of deleted IDs. Your own off-site copies follow the same rule (keep 30–90 days at most).

questions.q: Do external service providers have access to personal data?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Supabase (everything; its subprocessor AWS hosts it); Cloudflare (IP addresses and requests, no stored data); Google (Gmail sends sign-in codes; Google sign-in if used); Apple (Sign in with Apple, stores); Anthropic (only if the AI helper is deployed: topic, photo, drawing, dialect code); the device makers (dictation may send audio to Apple or Google; in Chrome on a computer, the "Google" voices are online voices, so the text being spoken is sent to Google). Later, with billing:
Apple and Google (purchases) and RevenueCat (purchase records, if used).

questions.q: Can external providers use collected data for their own purposes or AI training?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Check each contract. Supabase and Cloudflare act as processors. Anthropic's commercial API terms say API data is not used for training by default (confirm the current terms and retention period). A personal Gmail account is not covered by a business data-processing agreement: switch to Google Workspace or a transactional e-mail service with a DPA. Apple's and Google's speech services follow their own privacy policies: tell families, or prefer on-device dictation and offline voices.

questions.q: Who is the data controller and who is the data processor?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: The company is the controller for accounts, child profiles, follow-up data and analytics. A family using the app privately is not a controller. A therapist writing observations about patients may be a controller for those notes (or joint controller with the company). Schools and clinics usually want to be controllers with the company as their processor (art. 28 contract). Supabase, Cloudflare, Google and Anthropic are processors or subprocessors. The lawyer should fix this per customer type.

questions.q: What agreements are required with third-party providers and institutional customers?
questions.label: expert

bullets: Data-processing agreements with Supabase, Cloudflare, Google (Workspace), Anthropic, and later RevenueCat, with transfer clauses.
Institutions: not in the plan; if ever, a master agreement, order form, DPA with subprocessor list, security annex, service levels.
Professionals: terms of use with confidentiality.
US clinics that are covered entities: a HIPAA business associate agreement (Supabase offers HIPAA only on its Team plan with an add-on).

questions.q: What procedures must be followed in the event of a data breach?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: GDPR: notify the supervisory authority (CNIL) within 72 hours if there is a risk; inform the families without delay if the risk is high (likely, for children's data); keep an internal register of every incident. Saudi PDPL also has a 72-hour rule; US states and COPPA have their own. Prepare a one-page playbook (detect, contain, assess, notify, inform, fix, review) and message templates in French, English and Arabic.

sections.title: Cybersecurity
sections.in_short: The database decides who sees what (row-level security), every known attack is replayed by an automatic test, keys are never in the app, and the website sends strict browser protections. Gaps: no two-step sign-in for the team yet, sessions not in the phone's secure storage, no external penetration test, no written incident plan, and no staging step before changes go live.

questions.q: What cybersecurity standards does the application follow?
questions.label: app

answer.p: No formal certification. The design follows recognised practice: least privilege enforced by the database, the OWASP Top 10 for the website (Content-Security-Policy, no unsafe links, input cleaning), part of OWASP MASVS for mobile, security tests written as code, dependency audits.
Suggested targets: OWASP ASVS level 2 for the server and website, MASVS level 1 for the apps, ISO 27001-style policies later.

questions.q: Is the application aligned with OWASP MASVS recommendations?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Partly. Storage: sessions are kept in the app's storage, not yet in the iOS Keychain / Android Keystore; Android backups are off; device copies are erased at sign-out. Crypto: platform TLS only.
Authentication: strong server-side checks, 8-character passwords, rate limits; no two-step sign-in. Network: HTTPS only, HSTS on the website, no certificate pinning (acceptable at level 1).
Platform: links checked by one function (safeLink). Code: dependencies audited. Privacy: strong.
Gaps to close: Keychain/Keystore, two-step sign-in for the team, a mobile test by a professional.

questions.q: Is personal data encrypted during transmission and storage?
questions.label: app

answer.p: In transit: yes, HTTPS everywhere (Supabase, Cloudflare, strict transport security on the website).

At rest: Supabase encrypts its disks and backups (AES-256, on AWS). Inside the database, sensitive fields (sentences, observations) are not encrypted separately: worth considering. On devices: protected by the system's own encryption on modern iPads and Android tablets; browser storage on a shared computer is not.

questions.q: How are passwords and authentication credentials protected?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Passwords are handled by Supabase Auth: stored scrambled (bcrypt), never readable; minimum 8 characters (set the same minimum in the Supabase dashboard); e-mail confirmed by a code; rate-limited; optional leaked-password check on paid plans. Sessions are short-lived tokens plus a refresh token. The app holds only the public key; the powerful keys were never committed (checked in the whole history). The caregiver code (4 digits, pauses after wrong tries) protects against a child's hands, not against attackers.

questions.q: Is multifactor authentication available or mandatory for administrators?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Not yet in the app: Supabase supports authenticator-app codes for free, but there is no screen to enrol and the back office does not require it ("not done yet" in docs/SECURITY.md). Make it mandatory for the team (one check in is_admin() once enrolment exists: 1–2 days). Today, turn on two-step sign-in on Supabase, GitHub, Cloudflare and the Google accounts: whoever enters the Supabase account sees every child.

questions.q: Who has access to the production database?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Whoever is a member of the Supabase organisation (presumably only the owner today) or holds the database password or secret key. The app cannot: it only has the public key and the database's rules. Recommended: named members only, two-step sign-in, no shared accounts, rotate the secret key when someone leaves.

questions.q: How are administrator and developer permissions managed?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Back office: a database table (admins) that can only be changed in Supabase's SQL editor; every back-office function checks is_admin(). Developers: whoever has access to GitHub, Cloudflare and Supabase, which today look like the owner's personal accounts. To formalise: company-owned accounts, an access list, a quarterly review and a leaver checklist.

questions.q: Are administrative actions recorded in audit logs?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes for the back office: every decision on a certificate and every certificate opened goes into admin_log, which the app cannot erase. Profile changes have a history (who, when, what). Supabase keeps its own logs (1 day on the free plan, 7 days on Pro, longer on Team). Actions typed directly in Supabase's SQL editor are not in admin_log: keep that tool for emergencies.

questions.q: How do we prevent unauthorized access to user accounts and profiles?
questions.label: app

answer.p: In place: confirmed e-mails, rate limits, 8-character tablet codes with 5 tries, one code at a time, a notice to the family whenever a device is linked, remote removal of a lost device, copies erased at sign-out, "Keep me logged in" off for shared computers. To add: two-step sign-in as an option for parents, a robot check on sign-up (Cloudflare Turnstile, free), sessions in secure storage on tablets.

questions.q: How do we prevent unauthorized access between different families, professionals and institutions?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Row-level security on every table: a row is visible only to the profile's owner and its active members. Functions decide rights themselves and ignore any rights or owner sent by the app; professionals act only once verified; removed members lose access at once. 176 automatic checks replay the attacks (stranger, removed member, tablet, professional not verified). Known leftovers: team members can read each other's e-mail and the family code; whether an e-mail has an account can be guessed through invitations (limited to 30 a day).

questions.q: Are development, testing and production environments separated?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Partly: production Supabase project; a second Supabase project for live tests; a throw-away local database for security tests; the demo uses a fake server on the device. Today the repository's rule publishes every finished change to the website at once. Under the plan (native apps only) that rule changes: builds go to TestFlight and Google Play's testing tracks first, which serve as staging, then to the stores after review; the website keeps only the privacy and support pages.

questions.q: Are security vulnerabilities regularly identified and corrected?
questions.label: app

answer.p: One full internal review was done in November 2026: every finding was confirmed, fixed and turned into an automatic test. The dependency audit today reports 30 advisories in the production tree, all from three file-matching libraries used by build tools (picomatch, minimatch, glob via Metro and the Expo command line); none runs on families' devices. To set up: GitHub Dependabot and secret scanning (on the to-do list), Supabase's Security Advisor monthly, a quarterly review.

questions.q: Will independent penetration testing be conducted?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Recommended before selling (the security document says so too): an app about children's communication deserves an outside test. Scope: the server API and its rules (multi-family tests with real accounts), the iPad and Android apps, the back office inside the app.

questions.q: How frequently will security audits be performed?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Proposal: an external test once a year and after any major change to access rules; an internal review every quarter (access list, dependencies, Supabase advisor); every new database rule comes with its attack test (already the project's rule). ISO 27001 or SOC 2 only when institutions ask.

questions.q: What are the costs associated with cybersecurity maintenance and audits?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Penetration test €6,000–€20,000 a year; tools mostly free (Dependabot, Supabase advisor, Turnstile, authenticator codes); internal time 2–4 days a quarter; cyber insurance €1,000–€5,000 a year; optional certification (SOC 2 or ISO 27001) €20,000–€60,000 the first year, then €10,000–€30,000 a year.

questions.q: What is the incident response procedure in the event of a cyberattack?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: None is written yet. Draft: roles (incident lead: founder; technical: developer; legal: lawyer / DPO); severity levels; steps: contain (rotate keys, switch off functions, sign everyone out), keep the logs, assess what data was affected, notify within 72 hours, inform families in three languages, fix, review. Keep emergency contacts (Supabase support, CNIL, insurer). Practise once a year (two-hour table-top exercise).

questions.q: Do we need cybersecurity insurance?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Recommended. It pays for investigation, notification, legal defence and business interruption after a breach. About €1,000–€5,000 a year for a small company; insurers will ask about two-step sign-in, backups and updates, which are on the to-do list. Check that the cover includes all countries served.

sections.title: Accessibility
sections.in_short: The web build of the app passes an automatic WCAG 2.2 AA scan on 57 screens (204 scans, 0 failures), works with a keyboard, and is designed for screen readers. Under the plan only the native apps are offered, so the checks that matter now are on devices. Not done: listening with a real screen reader, any test on a tablet, and the access methods many AAC users rely on: switch scanning and eye gaze. Those are the main accessibility gaps.

questions.q: Which international accessibility standards apply to the application?
questions.label: app

answer.p: WCAG 2.2 level AA (the common reference); EN 301 549 in Europe (the harmonised standard, includes WCAG plus requirements for software, mobile apps, documentation and support); Section 508 and the ADA (US public buyers and services); RGAA (French public bodies); the Accessible Canada Act and Ontario's AODA; UK public-sector regulations.

questions.q: Which WCAG 2.2 AA and EN 301 549 requirements are applicable?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: All WCAG 2.2 A and AA criteria apply to the website; EN 301 549 chapter 11 applies the same ideas to the iPad and Android apps, plus: working with the system's accessibility services (11.5), following the user's system settings such as text size (11.7), and, because caregivers create content, the rules for authoring tools (11.8: the editor should help produce accessible content, e.g. a picture always has its word). Chapter 12: documentation and support must be accessible. Points to watch: dragging alternatives (2.5.7, done), target size (2.5.8), the caregiver code and memory (3.3.8), user text spacing (1.4.12), timers (2.2.1), animation (2.3.3).

questions.q: What are the mandatory accessibility requirements in each target country?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: For a private company selling to families, rarely mandatory for this kind of app: the European Accessibility Act covers listed products and services (an online shop selling subscriptions is one of them; very small companies are exempt for services). It becomes mandatory when selling to public bodies: EU public purchasing (EN 301 549), US Section 508 and ADA Title II (public schools), Canada and Ontario rules, Gulf government codes. Practical answer: meet WCAG 2.2 AA and publish a conformance report.

questions.q: Is the application compatible with VoiceOver and TalkBack?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Designed for them (names, roles and states on controls; each card tagged with its language so an Arabic word is read with an Arabic voice), and checked by program on the website. Never tested with real VoiceOver or TalkBack, because the native apps have not been built yet. Status: likely compatible, not verified.

questions.q: Is it compatible with switch access and scanning?
questions.label: app

answer.p: No built-in scanning. The iPad's Switch Control and Android's Switch Access work on any accessible app, so basic use may work, but it is untested and slow on a board of 60–81 cards. AAC-grade scanning (row/column, spoken preview, adjustable timing) is a real feature, important for users with motor impairments and offered by established AAC apps.
