questions.q: Is it compatible with eye-tracking technologies?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Not built in. iPadOS 18 and later include eye tracking with dwell that works across apps; on Android it depends on external devices. Untested.
Plan it together with switch scanning (dwell time, large targets, no accidental activation).

questions.q: Is it compatible with external keyboards and assistive devices?
questions.label: app

answer.p: On the website: yes, tested (Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, visible focus, panels as dialogs). On tablets: hardware keyboards work for typing; full keyboard control of the app is untested. Switch interfaces and other devices go through the system's accessibility features.

questions.q: Can users customize touch sensitivity, activation time and interaction methods?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, partly: select when the finger lifts, as soon as it touches, or by holding 0.5–2 seconds; a minimum delay between two presses of the same card (off, 1, 2, 3, 5 s); card sizes; larger text and high contrast; fewer animations; 25, 60 or 81 words shown. Missing: a touch area larger than the card, "first / last touch" choices for tremor, dwell for mouse and eye gaze.

questions.cost: 5–8 developer days for the missing ones

questions.q: Does the application meet visual contrast and readability requirements?
questions.label: app

answer.p: On the website, yes as far as a program can check: 22 colour pairs are computed by a unit test that fails if one drops under the rule; nine pairs were darkened; a high-contrast presentation exists; card colours are never the only clue. Large system font sizes on tablets are untested.

questions.q: Is it accessible to users with visual, motor, sensory and cognitive impairments?
questions.label: estimate

bullets: Cognitive: strong (words revealed progressively without moving, stable positions, simple guide, fewer animations, child lock).
Hearing: the sentence strip shows the text; timers are visual.
Motor: good for touch (hold to select, repeat delay); missing switch and eye gaze.
Visual: screen-reader names, contrast, zoom; missing auditory scanning for blind AAC users.

questions.q: Does it adequately support multilingual communication and right-to-left languages such as Arabic?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, as a design: words and menus have separate languages (French, English, Arabic); Arabic menus are mirrored but boards never are (motor plan); eight kinds of Arabic; mixing languages in one sentence; each card carries its language. Limits: the dialect word lists and the Arabic menus were not reviewed by native speakers; Arabic grammar is simple; no North African dialects; devices only speak Standard Arabic.

questions.q: Are tutorials, documentation and customer support accessible?
questions.label: app

answer.p: The in-app guide (30 chapters, three languages) and the set-up help are part of the scanned screens.
Missing: public help pages (with the privacy and support pages), captioned video tutorials, and a check that support e-mails and documents are accessible (EN 301 549 chapter 12).

questions.q: Will accessibility be tested with individuals with different disability profiles?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Not yet. Proposed first round: 5–8 AAC users (children with their speech therapist, adults), 5 caregivers, 3–5 speech therapists, 2–3 screen-reader users, 2 switch users, in French and Arabic.
Recruit through therapists and associations, with consent and fair pay.

questions.q: Do we need an independent accessibility audit?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Recommended before selling to institutions or claiming conformance: web + iPad + Android, with manual screen-reader tests.

questions.q: Do we need an accessibility statement or accessibility conformance report?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Yes: an accessibility statement on the static pages (expected in the EU) and a conformance report (VPAT 2.5 "INT" edition covers WCAG, Section 508 and EN 301 549) for public and institutional buyers.

questions.q: How will accessibility compliance be maintained after each update?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Already: npm run test:a11y (204 scans) and the contrast unit tests; the project rule says to run them after UI changes. Add them to a release checklist, plus a 30-minute screen-reader check per release and a yearly external re-audit.

questions.q: What are the costs associated with accessibility testing and compliance?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Audit €4,000–€15,000; user testing €3,000–€10,000 per round; conformance report €1,000–€5,000; switch and eye-gaze support 15–30 developer days; yearly upkeep €3,000–€10,000.

sections.title: App Store and Google Play distribution
sections.in_short: The plan of 18 November 2026 makes the stores the only sales channel: families subscribe monthly or yearly and therapists pay once, through Apple's and Google's in-app purchases. Nothing is on the stores yet: the native apps have never been built (the configuration still names the app "CAA" and has no bundle identifier). The store rules that matter most are listed in table A5b: in-app purchases with "Restore purchases" and a parental gate, a privacy policy (missing), Sign in with Apple (prepared), account deletion (done), the stores' privacy forms, and careful medical claims.

questions.q: What are the requirements for publishing the application on the App Store and Google Play?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Both: an organisation developer account, a privacy policy URL (missing today), a support URL, age rating, screenshots, a demo account for reviewers, account deletion inside the app (exists), permission texts in each language (today only French in app.json), the final app name (app.json still says "CAA") and identifiers (not set).

Apple: privacy "nutrition" label and privacy manifest, Sign in with Apple when Google sign-in is offered (prepared), in-app purchase for digital content (3.1.1), stricter review of medical apps (1.4.1).

Google: Data safety form, target-audience declaration (Families policy if children are part of the audience), health apps declaration, a web link to request account deletion, the current target Android version within a year of its release.

Under the plan, also: the in-app purchases themselves (subscriptions and the therapists' one-time purchase), "Restore purchases", and the purchase screen behind the caregiver code. The full list, with what exists, is table A5b.

questions.cost: 5–15 developer days for the first builds

questions.q: What are the initial and recurring developer account fees?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Apple Developer Program: US$99 a year (fee waivers exist for non-profits, educational institutions and government bodies in some countries). Google Play: US$25 once. Expo EAS builds: free to US$199 a month (US$19 is usually enough).

questions.q: Should developer accounts be registered under the company's name?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Yes. The seller's name shown on the store is then the company's; the company can be sold or transferred with its apps; and Google's organisation accounts avoid the "12 testers for 14 days" requirement imposed on new personal accounts. It needs a legal entity and a free D-U-N-S number (1–2 weeks). Moving an app from a personal account later is possible but cumbersome.

questions.q: What commissions will Apple and Google charge on purchases and subscriptions?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Apple: 30% standard; 15% in the Small Business Program (under US$1 million a year) and for subscriptions after their first year. New EU terms from 1 October 2026 (unified commission, lower rates for small developers and link-outs: check App Store Connect). In the US, purchases through an external link currently carry no Apple commission while a court sets a fee.
Google: 15% on subscriptions from day one; 15% on the first US$1 million a year for other purchases, 30% above.

questions.q: Can subscriptions be purchased directly through our website?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Possible, but not in the plan: everything is sold through the stores' in-app purchases, with no web checkout and no external payment link. Apple does allow using on the web what was bought in the app.

questions.q: Can subscriptions purchased on one platform be used on another platform?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, and the plan needs it: the right to use paid features is stored on the account, in Supabase (fed by the stores' or RevenueCat's notifications), not on the device. One family subscription then unlocks every device of the family, the linked tablet included, even across iPhone and Android; a therapist's one-time purchase follows her account to her other devices.

questions.q: Can users access their accounts across iOS, Android and web platforms?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, already: the same account works on iPad, iPhone and Android, and boards sync between them (the web app will not be offered under the plan). Photos and recordings do not sync (yet).

questions.q: Can different subscription prices be established for different countries?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes: both stores let you set prices per country (with automatic equalisation from one base price).
Consider lower prices for Lebanon and Egypt.

questions.q: Can institutional licences be sold outside the app stores?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Possible (Apple 3.1.3(c) allows invoicing organisations directly), but not in the plan: therapists buy their workspace once in the app.

questions.q: What are the additional requirements for applications used by children?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Apple Kids category (optional; it forbids third-party analytics and advertising and needs a parental gate): an AAC app used by all ages usually stays in Medical or Education. Google Families policy applies if children are part of the target audience. The app has no advertising and no tracker, and the caregiver code acts as a parental gate for purchases (to build). One gap: the app pictograms (YouTube, WhatsApp, Spotify…) open other apps from the child's board unless the child lock is on; under the Kids category or the Families policy, outside links must sit behind a parental gate (table A5b).

questions.q: What are the privacy and security requirements imposed by each platform?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Apple: privacy label, privacy manifest, account deletion, no tracking without permission (the app does not track), clear permission texts. Google: Data safety form (must match reality), account deletion in-app and on the web, justification of the microphone permission, encryption in transit.
Both: a privacy policy reachable in the app and on the store page.

questions.q: What could result in the rejection or removal of the application?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Missing privacy policy or terms; no "Restore purchases"; purchases a child can reach without a parental gate; medical claims without support; crashes on the reviewer's device; no working demo account; Sign in with Apple missing; unclear permission texts; a Data safety form that does not match the app; an outdated target Android version.

questions.q: What happens if a developer account is suspended?
questions.label: app

answer.p: The apps disappear from the store and cannot be updated; installed copies keep working (the board runs offline) but purchases and renewals stop, and under the plan that is all the revenue; there is no website to fall back on. Prevention: company accounts, two administrators with two-step sign-in, following the policies.

questions.q: Can we restrict the application's availability in specific countries?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes: both stores let you choose the countries per app.

questions.q: How are refunds, cancellations and subscription renewals managed?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Store purchases: people cancel in their Apple or Google settings; Apple decides refunds itself; Google lets you refund; the stores send renewal notices and retry failed payments. Under the plan there is no web purchase to manage. Policy suggestion: generous refunds, and never block communication.

sections.title: Intellectual property and ownership
sections.in_short: All code libraries and pictogram libraries allow commercial use; obligations are attribution (done for pictograms, to add for code libraries) and share-alike for modified Mulberry or OpenMoji drawings. The main ownership task is moving the code and accounts from personal accounts into the company, with written assignments. Voices are the device's own, so no voice licence is needed.

questions.q: Who legally owns the application's source code?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: The repository is on a personal GitHub account ("charbels07"). Copyright belongs to the human author(s). The code was produced with an AI coding tool under the owner's direction: the AI provider's terms give the customer the rights in the output, but copyright protection of purely machine-generated material is uncertain in some countries (the US requires human authorship), so protection also rests on the owner's own contributions, confidentiality and contracts.
To do: once the company exists, a written assignment of all rights from the founder (and any contributor) to the company, and move the repository to a company GitHub organisation.

questions.q: Who owns the application design, database, algorithms and documentation?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: The same author(s). The vocabulary, dialect lists, situation library and documentation are protected by copyright, and the database may also have the EU database right. Algorithms are not protected as such. If anyone else wrote parts (the original specification, word lists, reviews by a speech therapist), get their written assignment or licence.

questions.q: Does the company have full commercial rights to all developed components?
questions.label: app

answer.p: For third-party parts, yes: every code library and pictogram library allows commercial use (10.6, 10.7), ARASAAC was removed, Tawasol was excluded. For the company's own code, once the assignments of 10.1 are signed.

questions.q: Will the company have unrestricted access to the source code?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, once the repository is in the company's GitHub organisation. Also keep a mirror copy with a second provider and every key in a company password manager.

questions.q: Can another developer or development company take over the project?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes. The technologies are mainstream (TypeScript, React Native / Expo, PostgreSQL / Supabase) and the documentation is unusually complete (how each feature works, security, accessibility, keys, set-up, project rules and decisions in CLAUDE.md), with automatic tests. Plan a paid hand-over review of 5–10 days: the code base is large, written fast with AI help, and the native apps have never been built.

questions.q: Are all third-party libraries authorized for commercial use?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes. The production dependency tree has 523 packages: 449 MIT, 29 ISC, 10 BSD-2, 8 BSD-3, 6 Apache-2.0, 6 BlueOak and a few other permissive licences. Two build tools carry MPL-2.0 (lightningcss) and LGPL (sharp's WebAssembly build) but are not shipped inside the app; node-forge is dual BSD / GPL (BSD applies). Obligation: keep the licence notices: add an "Open-source licences" page for code libraries (only pictogram credits exist today).

questions.q: Are all pictogram libraries authorized for commercial use?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, according to each library's official source: Mulberry and OpenMoji (CC BY-SA 4.0), Twemoji (CC BY 4.0), Fluent Emoji, Phosphor, Tabler (MIT), Noto Emoji and Material Symbols (Apache 2.0), Lucide (ISC), Health Icons (CC0): 24,128 pictograms. ARASAAC (non-commercial) was removed; Tawasol excluded until Mada confirms its licence in writing. Seven points remain for a lawyer (store copy protection versus CC BY-SA, brand-named Mulberry symbols, Noto's two licence files…).

questions.q: Are all text-to-speech voices authorized for commercial use?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes in the sense that no voice is shipped: the app uses the device's own voices through the system (Apple, Android, browser), which is their intended use, free, with nothing redistributed. Families' recordings belong to them. The Azure dialect voices were not shipped. Do not record a system voice and ship the audio files.

questions.q: Are there restrictions on modifying, storing, distributing or exporting third-party resources?
questions.label: app

answer.p: CC BY-SA: a modified drawing must be marked and shared under the same licence; no technical measure may stop people using the licensed material (the store question). Mulberry: never sell the symbols themselves (no paid pictogram pack). Printing and exporting boards is fine with the credit line (already printed). Trademarks shown in icons are not licensed: brand logos were not imported.

questions.q: Are there mandatory attribution requirements?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, and they are met for pictograms: a credits page (Settings → About, the welcome page, the guide, the professional workspace) with full licence texts, and a credit line on every printed page. To add: notices for the code libraries and for Unicode CLDR (the emoji names).

questions.q: Are there restrictions based on the number of users or countries of distribution?
questions.label: app

answer.p: None in the open licences (worldwide, unlimited). Service terms (Supabase, Anthropic, stores) have no user caps but do exclude sanctioned countries. The app uses only standard encryption (HTTPS), correctly declared to Apple.

questions.q: Are there recurring licensing fees or royalties?
questions.label: app

answer.p: No: not for pictograms, code libraries or voices. Only service fees (section 11).

questions.q: What happens if a third-party provider changes its licensing conditions?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Open licences cannot be withdrawn for the versions already obtained, and the exact versions are pinned (pictograms/libraries.json) and can be downloaded again; keep a private archive of the originals in case a project disappears. Services (Supabase, Anthropic, stores) can change terms and prices: see 11.10.

questions.q: Who owns the content and communication boards created by users?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Write it in the terms: users keep ownership of what they create (photos, recordings, their own words and boards) and give the company only the licence needed to host and run the service; professionals own their materials and choose how they share them; the company owns its built-in vocabulary and templates and the anonymous statistics. In AAC, a person's vocabulary is their voice: make export easy.

questions.q: Should the company name, application name and logo be registered as trademarks?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Yes, after a clearance search: "Empower" is a common word in trademarks, so conflicts in software, education and health classes (9, 41, 42, 44) are possible. Note that the app's configuration still names it "CAA": settle the final brand before the store launch.

questions.q: In which countries should intellectual property protection be obtained?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Core markets: EU (one EUIPO filing for 27 countries), UK, US, Canada, Lebanon, UAE, Saudi Arabia.

The Madrid system (WIPO) covers most of them from one application; Lebanon is not a member (national filing), and Kuwait and Qatar need checking. Fees: EUIPO €850 for one class (+€50 the second, +€150 each further); UK £170 + £50 per class; USPTO about US$350 per class; Madrid base fee 653 CHF plus per-country fees; Gulf and Lebanon with agents US$500–2,500 per country.

questions.source: EUIPO, UKIPO, USPTO, WIPO fee lists

sections.title: Third-party services and technological dependencies
sections.in_short: The app depends mainly on Supabase (data, sign-in, files), with Cloudflare, Gmail and the device's own voice and dictation services around it, and Anthropic's AI ready but switched off. Because the board runs on the device, no outside service can stop a child from speaking on a device already set up. Supabase is the one hard dependency, made acceptable by its open-source nature and the SQL kept in the repository.

questions.q: Which third-party services, APIs, SDKs and libraries are integrated into the application?
questions.label: app

bullets: Supabase: sign-in, PostgreSQL database, file storage, server functions (caa-ai, caa-mail), scheduled jobs.
Cloudflare: today the web app; under the plan only the privacy and support pages.
Gmail (SMTP): sign-in codes and e-mails to the team.
Google sign-in (on), Sign in with Apple (prepared).
Anthropic API: the AI helper (written, not deployed).
Expo modules: speech, audio, camera and photos, printing, sharing, files, speech recognition, keep-awake.
The device's text-to-speech and speech recognition (Apple, Google, Microsoft in browsers).
GitHub: code hosting.
Later: Apple's and Google's in-app purchases (the plan: families subscribe, therapists pay once), RevenueCat, an e-mail service.

questions.q: What is the purpose of each external service?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Supabase: everything shared between devices and people. Cloudflare: serving the privacy and support pages.

Gmail: e-mails. Google / Apple sign-in: easier sign-in. Anthropic: word, step and photo suggestions and drawing recognition. Device voices: speaking. Device dictation: saying a word to search or dictating a sentence to model. Apple's and Google's in-app purchases, with RevenueCat: subscriptions and the therapists' purchase. Expo: building and updating the apps.

questions.q: What are their pricing models?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Supabase: plan plus usage. Cloudflare: free for static files. Gmail: free (limited). Google sign-in: free. Apple: yearly program fee. Anthropic: per token (words in and out). Expo: plan plus builds.
Apple and Google: 15% of each sale as a small developer (30% outside the programs). RevenueCat: percentage of revenue. E-mail services: monthly tiers by volume. SMS: per message.

questions.q: Are charges calculated per user, request, character, download or transaction?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Per sign-in account (Supabase, above 100,000 a month); per GB transferred and stored (Supabase); per compute hour (Supabase server size); per token (Anthropic: Opus 5.5 US$4 per million in, US$20 per million out; Haiku 5.5 US$0.10 / US$0.50); per e-mail (e-mail services); per transaction (the stores: 15% of each sale without VAT); per tracked revenue (RevenueCat 1%); per build (Expo). Per character only for cloud voices, which the app does not use.

questions.q: What are their free usage limits?
questions.label: app

answer.p: See 1.6. Key ones: Supabase free 50,000 accounts, 500 MB database, 5 GB transfer, no backups; Supabase Pro includes 100,000 accounts, 8 GB, 250 GB transfer; Cloudflare static free and unlimited; Gmail about 500 e-mails a day; RevenueCat free to US$2,500 a month; Expo a few free builds.

questions.q: Are there geographical restrictions?
questions.label: app

answer.p: US providers exclude sanctioned countries. The stores pay into a bank account in the company's name, and banking from Lebanon is difficult: a reason to choose the company's country carefully.
The AI requests leave from Supabase's servers, so the family's location does not matter for them.
The stores are available in all target countries.

questions.q: Do these services require internet access?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, all of them, except the device's voices (usually offline on iPad and Android; some browser voices are online) and on-device dictation where the system offers it. The board itself needs no internet in the native app.

questions.q: What personal data is transmitted to each provider?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Supabase: all shared data. Cloudflare: IP addresses and requests. Gmail: e-mail addresses and codes; the team e-mail includes a professional's name, profession and country. Google / Apple sign-in: name and e-mail. Anthropic: topic text, photo or drawing and a dialect code (never the child's name, words or sentences), but a photo may show people. Device services: dictated audio; in Chrome on a computer, the text read by "Google" voices.

questions.q: What happens if a third-party service becomes unavailable?
questions.label: app

bullets: Supabase down: boards keep working on devices already set up; changes wait and are sent later; sign-in, new devices, team actions and the back office stop.
Cloudflare down: the privacy and support pages are unreachable for a while; the apps are not affected.
Gmail down: no sign-up or password-reset codes.
Anthropic down: AI buttons fail; the built-in situation library still works.
Stores down: no installs or updates.

questions.q: What happens if a provider increases its prices?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Supabase: the stack is open source and the database is standard PostgreSQL, so self-hosting or moving is possible (2.14); keeping usage efficient (done for the 30-second check on 17 November 2026) limits exposure. Anthropic: change model or cap usage. Stores: commissions are set by policy and courts, not negotiable.
RevenueCat: can be replaced by direct store integration.

questions.q: Can external services be replaced without major redevelopment?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Cloudflare: trivial (static files). Gmail: trivial (SMTP settings). Anthropic: small (one function, portable prompts). RevenueCat: medium. Supabase: moderate (5–15 days to self-host Supabase, 10–25 days to move to plain PostgreSQL with another sign-in service). Expo / React Native: high (it is the app's framework, but open source).

questions.q: Are there free, commercially licensed or locally hosted alternatives?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Self-hosted Supabase (Apache 2.0) on OVHcloud, Scaleway or Hetzner (some with HDS certification); static hosting on Netlify, OVH or any object storage; European e-mail services (Brevo, Mailjet) or Amazon SES; open-weight AI models hosted in the EU (lower quality, more work); for purchases, the stores' own libraries instead of RevenueCat; device voices are already free and local; analytics are already the app's own.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: How dependent is the application on a single technology provider?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Most dependent on Supabase (data, sign-in, files, functions): mitigated by open source, SQL in the repository and off-site backups. Then on Expo / React Native (open source framework) and the two stores (the plan's only sales channel; there is no web fallback). Write a short migration runbook and avoid adding Supabase-only features without need.

sections.title: Business model, payments and taxation
sections.in_short: The plan (set on 18 November 2026): the app is sold only inside the iPad / iPhone and Android apps, through Apple's and Google's in-app purchases. Families take an auto-renewing subscription, monthly or yearly; therapists buy the professional workspace once. Nothing is sold on the web. The stores then collect VAT and sales tax in most countries, take payment, send receipts and handle refunds; they keep 15% of each sale without VAT as a small developer (Apple once you enrol in its Small Business Program). Billing is not built yet. The company's country is a decision for an accountant; it needs a bank account the stores can pay into.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate country for establishing the company?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: A decision for the founder with an accountant. Criteria: where the founders live and manage the company (that decides tax residence), the first market, access to a bank account the stores can pay into, public funding, and regulation (an EU company needs no EU representative for the GDPR or the MDR).

bullets: France (SAS): natural for an EU and French-speaking start; corporate tax 15% up to €42,500 of profit then 25%; innovation support (Bpifrance, the young innovative company status, research and innovation tax credits).
UAE free zone: 0% on qualifying income, 9% standard above AED 375,000; strong for the Gulf, weaker as an EU health-data controller.
Lebanon: useful as a local presence, but banking is difficult and many payment services do not serve Lebanese companies.

answer.p: A common path: an EU company first, a Gulf branch or distributor later.

questions.q: What business licences are required to sell the application internationally?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Usually none beyond company registration: under the plan, Apple and Google sell the app to the user in each country. Exceptions: medical-device registrations if the app is one (section 5).

questions.q: What corporate taxes apply?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Those of the company's country (France 15% / 25%; UAE 0% / 9%; UK 19–25%; Lebanon 17%; Saudi 20% on the foreign-owned share), on the proceeds the stores pay you. The stores deal with the taxes on each sale (12.4); corporate tax on the profit stays yours.

questions.q: What VAT or sales tax obligations apply in each country?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Digital services sold to consumers are taxed where the customer lives (EU VAT 17–27%; UK 20%; US sales tax in many states; Canada GST/HST and QST; Saudi Arabia 15%, UAE 5%, Bahrain 10%, Oman 5%, Egypt 14%, Lebanon 11%). Under the plan, Apple and Google collect and pay these taxes in most countries: store prices include VAT, and you receive the price minus VAT minus the store fee. The consoles (App Store Connect, Play Console) list the few countries where the developer must handle it.
In the company's own country you still declare VAT on your own purchases and the stores' invoices, with your accountant.

questions.source: App Store and Google Play tax terms; national rules

questions.q: Who is responsible for collecting and remitting these taxes?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Apple and Google, for every sale in the app, in most countries (see 12.4). Not in the plan: web sales, where the company (or a reseller) would be responsible.

questions.q: Do we need to register for tax purposes in multiple countries?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Under the plan, usually not for the sales: the stores account for the tax in the buyer's country. The company registers where it is established (VAT, corporate tax). Ask the accountant to check the consoles' list of countries where the developer is responsible.

questions.q: What payment processing solutions are available?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Under the plan: Apple's and Google's in-app purchases only. To build (billing, table A5):

bullets: In-app purchases in the app, through RevenueCat (free up to US$2,500 of monthly tracked revenue, then 1%) or a direct store library.

A server-side entitlement in Supabase, fed by the stores' or RevenueCat's notifications: one family subscription unlocks every device of the family, the linked tablet included, even across iPhone and Android.
A "Restore purchases" button (Apple requires it).
The purchase screen behind the caregiver code: a child uses the board, so buying needs a parental gate.
The therapist's one-time purchase tied to her account on the server, so her other devices get it too.

answer.p: Not in the plan: Stripe or another web checkout, external payment links.

questions.source: App Store Review Guidelines 3.1.1, 3.1.2; Google Play billing policy

questions.q: Which payment methods should be supported in each target market?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Nothing to integrate: Apple and Google offer their users each country's usual ways to pay (cards, their own wallets, store gift cards, and in some countries mobile-operator billing or local methods).
Store gift cards matter in Lebanon, where many cards cannot pay abroad.

questions.q: What are the transaction and currency conversion fees?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Only the stores' commission, which includes payment processing and currency conversion:

bullets: Apple: 15% in the Small Business Program (proceeds under US$1 million a year; you must enrol), otherwise 30%; auto-renewing subscriptions drop to 15% after a subscriber's first paid year. EU: new terms from 1 October 2026 (see 9.4).
Google Play: 15% on subscriptions from day one; 15% on the first US$1 million a year of other sales (the therapists' one-time purchase), 30% above.
RevenueCat, if used: 1% above US$2,500 of monthly tracked revenue.

answer.p: At the report's example prices (France, 20% VAT): €1.25 a month for a €9.99 monthly subscription, €10.00 a year for a €79.99 yearly one; 15% of the price without VAT for the therapists' purchase, whose price is not set yet (table A6).

questions.cost: 15% of each sale without VAT (30% outside the programs)
questions.source: Apple and Google commission rules; Apple newsroom (Aug 2026)

questions.q: How will international payments be transferred to the company's bank account?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Apple pays monthly (about 45 days after the end of the month), Google monthly, each in your account's currency. A multi-currency business account (Wise, Revolut Business) cuts conversion costs. Avoid an account in Lebanon for receiving funds.

questions.q: Are there restrictions on receiving payments from specific countries?
questions.label: app

answer.p: The stores do not sell in sanctioned countries; you also choose the countries in each store (check Syria's status at the time). Lebanese buyers whose cards cannot pay abroad can use store gift cards.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: How will invoices and receipts be generated?
questions.label: app

answer.p: The stores send receipts to buyers; you do not invoice them. You receive the stores' monthly financial reports and their invoices for the commission, for your accounting. France's electronic invoicing between companies (receiving from September 2026, issuing from September 2027 for small companies) concerns invoices between companies established in France: your accountant handles it.

questions.q: How will institutional purchases be invoiced?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Not in the plan: therapists buy their workspace once in the app. If schools or clinics later want to buy for their staff, Apple allows selling to organisations outside the store (3.1.3(c)), by invoice: a separate decision.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: What are the financial implications of monthly, annual and lifetime subscriptions?
questions.label: estimate

bullets: Families, monthly (the report's example: €9.99): flexible, more churn; 15% to the store each month.

Families, yearly (example: €79.99, a third less than 12 months): cash up front, less churn; 15% once a year. On Apple, subscriptions drop to 15% after a subscriber's first paid year even outside the Small Business Program.

Therapists, one-time purchase (non-consumable): money once, but servers, support and updates continue for as long as she uses it, so the price has to cover years of use. It must be restorable on her other devices ("Restore purchases" and the account on the server). Its price is not set yet.
A lifetime purchase for families: not in the plan.

questions.q: What are the financial implications of offering a free version?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: The plan does not say what a family can use without paying. The app already promises: "Whatever happens, the child will always be able to communicate" (15.5). Two ways that fit the stores: a free trial (an introductory offer of the subscription), or a free communication core with the subscription for the adult tools (team and sync, follow-up, several children, AI if switched on). Free users cost little in servers (about €0.01 a month); support is the real cost.

questions.q: How will free trials, promotional codes and discounts be managed?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Apple: introductory offers (free trial, reduced first period), offer codes, promotional offers for past subscribers. Google: free trials, introductory prices, promo codes. RevenueCat manages offers across both stores. Discounts for therapists: a temporary lower price, or the stores' promotional codes where they allow them for one-time purchases.

questions.q: How will refunds, chargebacks and failed payments be managed?
questions.label: app

answer.p: All through the stores: Apple decides refunds itself (you can send it usage information), Google lets you refund; both retry failed renewals and offer a grace period; there are no card chargebacks to handle yourself. Rule to write into the terms and the code: when a payment fails, communication keeps working fully; only paid extras pause after the grace period.

sections.title: Financial forecasting and profitability
sections.in_short: The figures below are a model, not a forecast, built on the plan of 18 November 2026: families subscribe monthly or yearly in the stores, therapists pay once. Prices, the monthly / yearly mix, the therapists' price and growth are your decisions. The key result: servers cost cents and the stores keep 15%, so break-even depends on fixed costs. With about €60,000 a year of fixed costs and a €9.99 monthly family subscription, about 750 paying families are enough; with a small salaried team (€250,000 a year), about 3,100. Therapists' one-time purchases come on top (not modelled: price and number not set).

questions.q: What is the total initial investment required?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: One-off launch budget €48,000–€147,000 if you hire a developer for the development work, about €28,000–€101,000 in cash if you build it yourself (that cash is mostly outside professionals: lawyer, audits, reviews, insurance) (Part A, table A5); add €25,000–€80,000 for an EU class I medical-device route; plus 6–12 months of running costs as a buffer (13.2).

questions.q: What is the minimum annual budget required to operate the application without generating revenue?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: "Keep it alive" mode, founder doing development and support: servers €600–1,500, Apple €90, domain and e-mail €300, accountant €1,500–3,500, insurance €1,500–6,000, DPO / legal €3,000–10,000:
€8,000–€25,000 a year. With a part-time developer and yearly audits:

questions.q: What is the cost per free active user?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Servers about €0.01 a month (since the refresh fix of 17 November 2026), support €0.05–0.30 a month depending on how much people help themselves with the guide: about €0.10–0.35 a month, or €1–4 a year.

questions.q: What is the cost per paying active user?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Servers as above, plus the store fee (15% of the price without VAT; 30% outside the programs), RevenueCat 1%, AI if included (€0.05–0.20 a month), more support. For a €9.99 monthly subscription: about €2.00–3.50 a month in total.

questions.q: What is the net revenue generated by each subscription after commissions, taxes and operating costs?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Worked example, French customer, 20% VAT, store fee 15% (Apple's Small Business Program; Google Play subscriptions), prices of the report's examples. Revenue = price − VAT − store fee:

bullets: Family monthly €9.99 → €8.33 without VAT → minus the store €1.25 → minus RevenueCat €0.10 → €6.98; minus servers and support €0.30 → €6.68 a month.
Family yearly €79.99 → €66.66 without VAT → minus the store €10.00 and RevenueCat €0.80 → €55.86 a year (€4.65 a month); minus €0.30 a month → €4.35.
Therapist, one-time price P (not set yet): about 0.70 × P once (P ÷ 1.2, minus 15%, minus 1% of P); servers and support then cost about €0.30 a month for as long as she uses it.

answer.p: If Apple's Small Business Program is not used, Apple takes 30%: €5.73 a month and €45.86 a year in the first year of a subscription, back to the 15% figures from the second paid year.

questions.q: What is the minimum subscription price required to remain profitable?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Price (VAT included, France, store at 15%) ≈ (yearly fixed costs ÷ 12 ÷ paying users + €0.30) ÷ 0.70.
So the price follows the number of payers you can realistically reach, and the size of the team.

questions.q: How many paying users are required to reach the break-even point?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Paying families needed = yearly fixed costs ÷ 12 ÷ (net per family per month − €0.30).
With a €79.99 yearly subscription (net €4.35 a month): €60,000 → 1,149; €250,000 → 4,789.
With a mix of both, the answer lies in between (the mix is not known yet). Each therapist's one-time purchase lowers it; not counted here because its price and the number of therapists are not set.

questions.q: What percentage of free users must convert into paying users?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: It depends on what a family can use without paying, which the plan does not say yet (12.15). With a free trial only, every family that keeps the app after the trial pays. With a free core: conversion = paying families needed ÷ active families; for example 749 out of 20,000 is 3.7%, out of 10,000 it is 7.5%. Consumer apps with a free version often convert 2–5%; families with a strong need may convert more if the paid part is clearly valuable. Therapists pay once to use the workspace.

questions.q: What are the projected revenues and expenses over the first three to five years?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Not something I can predict without your prices, marketing budget and markets. Build the model with these drivers: new active families per month and per market, share paying, monthly / yearly mix, net revenue after VAT and the stores' 15%, churn, cost of acquiring a family; therapists: number and one-time price (not set); and costs: team, compliance, servers per user.
Illustration only (not a forecast): 500 / 2,000 / 5,000 paying families at €6 net a month → revenue about €36,000 / €144,000 / €360,000 a year, against costs of perhaps €60,000 / €150,000 / €300,000.

questions.q: How does profitability change as the number of users increases?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: It improves strongly: servers grow slowly and stay small, fixed costs do not grow, support grows in steps (one more person every few thousand families). The danger is a per-use cost included in a flat price without limits: the AI helper.

questions.q: Which features generate the highest operating costs?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Servers: no single large item since the 30-second refresh was made light (17 November 2026); the largest server line at scale is sign-in accounts above 100,000 a month. If switched on: the AI helper (money). In people: verifying professionals (manual), support for set-up and team features, native-speaker content reviews.

questions.q: Which countries offer the highest profitability?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Highest prices and largest AAC market: the US (but heavy privacy rules and strong competitors).

Then the UK, France / EU, Canada (French and English) and the Gulf (high purchasing power, and the app's Arabic dialects are a real advantage, but medical-device registration and localisation cost more). Lebanon is a mission market more than a profit market (low purchasing power, payment problems). The real answer will come from revenue by store country once billing exists.

questions.q: What financial reserves should be maintained for unexpected expenses?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: 6–12 months of fixed costs, plus €10,000–€20,000 for an incident (breach response, urgent legal advice), plus a regulatory reserve if the CE route is chosen.

questions.q: What are the financial risks associated with different subscription models?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Monthly subscriptions: churn. Yearly: refund requests through the stores. Therapists' one-time purchase: money once, costs for years; its price must cover them. All revenue goes through two stores: their commission or policy changes, and an account suspension (9.13), hit everything at once. If there is a free part: low conversion. Funders often prefer one-time purchases. Currency risk between EUR, USD and local currencies (the stores pay in your currency at their rates).

sections.title: Maintenance and technical support
sections.in_short: Today one person maintains everything, through AI-assisted development sessions, with no contract, no staging step and accounts that look personal. The documentation and automatic tests are good enough for someone else to take over; the gaps are organisational: company-owned accounts, a backup developer, a release process and a maintenance agreement.

questions.q: Who will be responsible for maintaining the application after launch?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Today the owner, through AI-assisted development sessions; there is no maintenance contract. Choose: an in-house developer, a freelancer on retainer, or an agency; and name a backup.

questions.q: What is included in the maintenance agreement?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Suggested contents: bug fixes by severity; security patches; framework upgrades (Expo 2–3 times a year); yearly iOS, Android and browser compatibility; store policy and Android target updates; checking backups and monitoring; small improvements (X days a month); keeping documentation and the guide up to date; on-call for critical incidents; help with data-protection requests.

questions.q: What are the monthly and annual maintenance costs?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Freelancer 3–5 days a month: €1,500–€3,500 a month (€18,000–€42,000 a year). Agency: €3,000–€8,000 a month. Salaried developer in France: €45,000–€70,000 gross, about €65,000–€100,000 with charges.

questions.q: What is the expected response time for technical incidents?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Proposal for a small team: critical (communication impossible for many users, data leak): acknowledged within 2 hours, including evenings and weekends during the launch period; major: 1 business day; minor: next release.

questions.q: What is the expected resolution time for critical bugs?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Workaround within 24 hours, fix within 72 hours. Under the plan (native apps only) every fix waits for store review, about 1 to 3 days (Apple offers expedited review for critical bugs), instead of minutes for the website; an over-the-air update service (Expo EAS Update) allows fast fixes to the app's JavaScript within the stores' rules.

questions.q: Who is responsible for compatibility with new iOS and Android versions?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: The maintainer, by contract. Calendar: Apple betas in June, release in September; Google raises the required Android target every August. Each needs testing and usually an Expo upgrade.

questions.q: How frequently will updates be released?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Proposal: native apps a monthly fix release and a quarterly feature release; announced in the app in three languages. Never re-arrange a child's board in an update.

questions.q: How will updates be tested before deployment?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Existing: type check, 300 unit tests, 176 database checks, the accessibility suite, browser walkthroughs. Missing: tests on real tablets, a staging site, beta testers (TestFlight, Google closed testing), a written release checklist (19.10).

questions.q: Can unsuccessful updates be rolled back?
questions.label: app

answer.p: No website under the plan. Database changes: forward-only files; write reversible changes and take a backup before each. Native apps: a store version cannot be withdrawn, only replaced; use phased releases (Apple over 7 days, Google staged rollout) and over-the-air fixes.

questions.q: Is the source code fully documented?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Well documented for a project of this size: how each feature works and where (docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md, 35 rounds), security, accessibility, keys and services, pictogram licences, server set-up, project rules and the owner's decisions (CLAUDE.md), comments in the code. Missing: an architecture diagram, runbooks (deploy, restore, incident), an onboarding guide for a new developer.

questions.q: Does the company have independent access to all technical accounts and infrastructure?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Not yet, as far as the repository shows: GitHub is a personal account, the e-mails go through a Gmail account, and Supabase and Cloudflare are probably personal. The company should own: a GitHub organisation, a Supabase organisation, Cloudflare, Apple and Google developer accounts, the domain, company e-mail, Anthropic and Expo, each with two administrators and a company password manager.

questions.q: What happens if the current developer is no longer available?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Today a high risk: one person plus an AI tool. What already helps: thorough documentation, tests, mainstream technologies, and boards that keep working offline (communication would continue for weeks without maintenance). To do: give a second trusted person access, identify a backup freelancer who knows Expo and Supabase, write runbooks.

questions.q: What procedures are in place to transfer maintenance to another development team?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: None written. Checklist: repository and account access, rotating keys, setting up from the README, running every test suite, deploying to staging, a walk-through of architecture and decisions (CLAUDE.md), the list of open issues, 5–10 days of paid overlap.

questions.q: What service-level agreements should be established?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Under the plan there are no institutional contracts: publish targets for families and therapists rather than contractual SLAs: availability of the server side 99.5% a month (boards work offline anyway), support response times by severity, recovery targets (data loss at most 24 hours, service back within 8 hours), security notification within 48–72 hours. Supabase itself only offers an SLA on its Team and Enterprise plans: do not promise more than your providers give you.

sections.title: Reliability and AAC-specific considerations
sections.in_short: The app was designed so that the child can always speak: the board runs on the device, works without internet, and core word positions never move. The weak points are photos and recordings (only on one device), the native apps (never built or tested on devices yet), the lack of whole-board snapshots and of an export format other AAC apps can read, and the absence (so far) of a written promise about payment failures and discontinuation.

questions.q: Can the application function without an internet connection?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes on tablets and phones: the board, the built-in words and the 24,128 pictograms are inside the app; speech uses the device's voices (offline on iPad; on Android once the voice data is downloaded); recordings are on the device; changes wait and sync later.
The web app was weaker (it needs internet to start; some computer voices are online), but under the plan (native apps only, decided 18 November 2026) it is not offered, so that weakness disappears.

questions.q: Which features require an internet connection?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Sign-in and sign-up, linking a tablet, syncing changes, team features (invitations, proposals, history), sending follow-up data, the back office, AI suggestions and drawing search, professional verification, notices; dictation (usually).

questions.q: Can users continue communicating if the servers are unavailable?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, on every device already set up and signed in: the board works from its own copy, and changes are sent when the server is back. New sign-ins and new devices have to wait.

questions.q: Can users continue communicating if a third-party service becomes unavailable?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes: speech, pictograms and the board do not depend on Supabase, Cloudflare, Gmail or Anthropic on a native device. One real risk: a device without a voice for the language (e.g. an Android tablet without the Arabic voice installed) cannot speak; the set-up should check that the voice exists and explain how to install it.

questions.q: Can users access essential communication features if their subscription expires or a payment fails?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Billing is not built, and the app already says "Whatever happens, the child will always be able to communicate". Under the plan (a family subscription in the stores), make it binding: in the terms, and in the code (the server-side entitlement must never gate the board, speech, existing vocabulary, basic word editing, export or printing; only paid extras pause after the stores' grace period). This is an ethical and reputational must in AAC.

questions.q: How can users recover their communication boards if their device is lost, damaged or replaced?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Words, boards, settings, schedules and the team are on the server: sign in on the new device, or link a tablet with a code, and everything returns. Photos and recordings made on the lost device are lost (not synced; Android backups are switched off on purpose; an iPad's iCloud backup may hold them). Also possible: re-import an exported profile file; printed boards as a paper backup.

questions.q: Can personalized vocabulary and settings be transferred between devices?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes: through the account (automatic sync), a tablet code, the profile file (export / import), or a sibling's board as a starting point in the set-up. Photos and recordings: not yet.

questions.q: How will established pictogram positions and motor patterns be preserved during updates?
questions.label: app

answer.p: By design and by rule: core cells never move (a project rule), showing more words never moves the others, new built-in folders only go into empty places, activity boards are re-arranged only when a caregiver asks, the "no holes" display is display-only and the family can choose "final places".
Add a release test that compares the core layout before and after each update, and tell families about anything visible that changes.

questions.q: Can users restore previous versions of their communication boards?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Partly: the change history lets the family undo any single change. There is no "restore the board as it was on 3 March" and no list of saved versions; server backups are for disasters only.
Recommendation: automatic snapshots (weekly and before big changes, keep 10) with one-tap restore.

questions.q: How can accidental deletion or modification of communication boards be prevented?
questions.label: app

answer.p: In place: the caregiver code before any editing; the child lock; professionals propose and parents approve; core positions always need approval; confirmation before deleting on the main board; typing a word before deleting a profile or account; "Undo" after moving a card; undo from the history.
Missing: a bin for deleted words and boards, and a 30-day delay before a deleted child profile is really erased (today it is immediate).

questions.q: Can communication boards be exported in a usable and accessible format?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes: the profile file (the app's own JSON format), printed boards and PDF (A6 / A3, black and white, cut cards), CSV for observations and follow-up. Not yet: the Open Board Format (OBF / OBZ), the open exchange format several AAC apps can import, which would let a family move to another AAC system.

questions.q: What is our responsibility if a technical failure prevents a user from communicating?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Legally it depends on the terms, consumer law, product liability and, if it is a medical device, the MDR. The new EU Product Liability Directive treats software as a product from 9 December 2026, with strict liability for defects causing injury or loss of private data. You cannot exclude liability for injury caused by negligence. In practice: offline design, encourage a low-tech backup (printed board) during set-up, clear guidance to keep another way to communicate, insurance, and a fast incident process.

questions.q: How will continuity of communication be ensured if the application is discontinued?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Publish a continuity pledge: at least 12 months' notice; installed apps keep working offline; exports (PDF, profile file, and OBZ once built); refunds of unused prepaid periods; source code in escrow for institutions, or released under an open licence as a last resort.

sections.title: Customer support and user management
sections.in_short: The basics exist inside the app: a three-language guide, a "?" on every set-up question, a form to write to the team, votes on ideas, notices, and automatic problem counts. To add: a help desk, a public help page, a status page, and a privacy-respecting way for support to look at a family's board (invite support temporarily, as a team member).

questions.q: What customer support infrastructure is required?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: A shared help-desk inbox (free tiers, then €15–50 per agent a month), a public help centre (reusing the guide), the in-app "Help us improve Empower" form (exists, read in the back office), a status page (free tiers), reply templates in French, English and Arabic, an incident register.

questions.q: Who will provide technical support?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: At first the founder, with the developer for difficult cases; later a first-line support person who escalates to the developer.

questions.q: Who will respond to AAC-related questions?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: A speech-language therapist (part-time or by the hour, €40–€80 an hour), plus the guide and a network of partner therapists. Keep a clear line: general advice on using the app, not individual clinical advice, unless it is offered as a professional service.

questions.q: In which languages will support be available?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: French, English and Arabic (the app's languages); Arabic support should understand the dialects, starting with Lebanese.

questions.q: What customer support channels should be established?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: In-app form (exists), e-mail, help centre, WhatsApp Business (very common in Lebanon and the Gulf; mind privacy: no child data in chats), webinars for professionals, captioned video tutorials; no phone line needed under the plan.

questions.q: What are the estimated support costs per active user?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Early on, about one ticket per 20–50 active families a month, 10–15 minutes each: about €0.10–0.30 per active family a month at €25 an hour; more at launch and for teams, less as the guide improves.

questions.q: What response times can be guaranteed?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Proposal: free users (if any) 2–3 business days; subscribing families and therapists 1 business day; communication impossible: the same day.

questions.q: How will user complaints and technical incidents be documented?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Already: messages by subject (Requests page) and technical problems (Bugs page) in the back office.
Add: help-desk ticket numbers, an incident register (date, impact, cause, fix) and a complaints register (required by medical-device rules if the app becomes one).

questions.q: How will users report bugs and suggest improvements?
questions.label: app

answer.p: In the app: "Help us improve Empower" (six subjects, including problems and ideas) and votes on ideas written by the team (one vote per account). Automatically: technical problems counted from consenting families. And e-mail.

questions.q: How will users be informed about technical incidents, maintenance and updates?
questions.label: app

answer.p: In-app notices exist (written in three languages). To add: a status page, a "what's new" note in the app, store release notes, and e-mail through a proper e-mail service (today only sign-in codes are e-mailed).

questions.q: Can customer support access user accounts without compromising privacy?
questions.label: app

answer.p: The back office deliberately shows no child's content, and there is no "log in as the user" tool: good. To help a family, use what already exists: the family invites a support account into the child's team, with a role, a level and an end date (for example one week), or sends an exported file. Never read the database directly without the family's agreement; log every access.

questions.q: How will account recovery and password resets be managed?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Password reset by e-mailed code (exists); Google sign-in; a tablet is re-linked with a new code from a parent's device. Define a procedure for someone who lost access to their e-mail (identity check, confirmation by another parent or team member).

Forgotten caregiver code: added on 17 November 2026, extended on 18 November (pull request #6): the parent can also prove it with the account's password; Google and Apple accounts use the e-mailed code. Before, the code was changed in Settings, which is itself behind the code, so a family that forgot it was locked out. Now "Forgot the code?" under the keypad sends a code to the signed-in parent's e-mail or phone (the password-reset code), checks it without changing the password, and lets the family choose a new code. A professional does the same for her own code; a linked tablet is told to do it from a parent's device. The new e-mail text was pasted in Supabase on 18 November; its subject line still says only "New password".

sections.title: Professional and institutional licences
sections.in_short: Professionals are well served already: verified accounts, many children per professional, teams, proposals, materials and a hand-over of a prepared profile to the parents. Under the plan of 18 November 2026 each therapist buys the workspace once, in the app, tied to her account so all her devices get it. Therapists work on a tablet or phone (the web app is not offered, so no computer). Institutions as such (a school or clinic with seats, an administrator, invoices) do not exist and are not in the plan. The design choice that the child's profile belongs to the family is the right default for AAC.

questions.q: Can schools, clinics, hospitals and other organizations purchase multiple licences?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Not in the plan: each therapist buys the workspace once in the app, with her own verified account.
There is no organisation account, seat or invoice. If organisations ask later, Apple allows selling to them outside the store (3.1.3(c)); that would be a separate decision.

questions.cost: Organisation accounts, if ever: 15–30 developer days
questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: Can institutions centrally manage users and subscriptions?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Not in the plan. It would need an organisation console (staff, seats, children, transfers) and, later, single sign-on with Google Workspace or Microsoft.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: Can professionals manage multiple AAC user profiles?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes: "My AAC users", a materials library, drafts and proposals per child, and creating a child's profile to hand over to the parents with a code.

questions.q: Can multiple professionals collaborate on the same profile?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes: a team per child with roles, levels and permissions; proposals reviewed by the family; history with undo; shared materials (view or edit).

questions.q: How are permissions and responsibilities managed within an institution?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Per child, by the family (roles, levels, permissions, end dates). There is no institution-level hierarchy (for example a head of service seeing every child). If added, the family must still decide who sees its child's data.

questions.q: Can a user's profile be transferred when they change professionals or institutions?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, naturally: the profile belongs to the family; the former professional is removed (access cut at once, invitations cancelled) and the new one invited; materials can be shared or copied. A profile created by a professional is handed to the parents with a code.

questions.q: Who owns and controls the user's data when an institutional subscription ends?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Not in the plan (no institutional subscription). If it ever is, with today's model: the family keeps its child's profile; the institution loses access; the institution keeps its own materials. To decide: profiles an institution created for children whose families have no account (hand over before the end, or export and delete). Write it in the contract.

questions.q: What specific contracts are required for institutional customers?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Not in the plan. If organisations are ever sold to: a master service agreement, order form, data-processing agreement with subprocessor list and security annex, service levels, accessibility conformance report, acceptable use rules; for health bodies, proof of HDS hosting (France) or a HIPAA business associate agreement (US); public procurement terms.

questions.q: What additional privacy, security and accessibility requirements apply to institutional sales?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Not in the plan. If it changes: security questionnaires, a penetration test summary, help with their DPIA, a statement of where data is stored, an accessibility conformance report, staff training, audit logs, single sign-on and two-step sign-in, data export at the end of the contract.

questions.q: Do institutional customers require specific certifications, such as ISO 27001 or SOC 2?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Not needed under the plan (no institutional sales). If that changes, some will (hospitals, large school districts, US enterprises); small clinics and schools usually accept a questionnaire and a penetration test report. Start by relying on Supabase's own SOC 2 report (available on its Team plan) and your written policies; certify (€20,000–€60,000 the first year) when real deals require it. In France, health customers will ask about HDS hosting.

questions.q: What pricing models are appropriate for professionals and institutions?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Set by the plan: a one-time in-app purchase per therapist for the workspace (a non-consumable purchase, restorable on her other devices). Its price is not set yet: it has to cover years of servers, support and updates (13.5 shows what the company keeps: about 0.70 × the price in France).
Seats, site licences or school pricing are not in the plan.

questions.q: Are there opportunities for public procurement, government funding or healthcare reimbursement?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: France: the UGAP public purchasing catalogue, adapted school equipment funded through the MDPH, hospital tenders, Bpifrance and EU innovation grants. UK: NHS frameworks, Department for Education.

US: school districts (assistive technology in pupils' education plans), Medicaid and Medicare for speech-generating devices through equipment suppliers. Canada: provincial device programmes. Gulf: ministries of education and health, disability bodies (e.g. in the UAE and Saudi Arabia). Lebanon:
NGOs and UN agencies. Foundations funding assistive technology.
