sections.title: Product analytics and administrative back office
sections.in_short: A back office with seven pages already exists, built on a strict rule: the app should know its features very well and families' lives as little as possible. Figures from children come only from families who agreed, only as sums over at least 5 children of 5 families, never a name, word or sentence. Revenue, subscription, store and cost figures will come once billing and the stores exist.

questions.q: What information should be available in the administrative back office?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Already there: Professionals (verification requests), Administration (accounts, profiles, devices, professionals, teamwork: counts), Product (each feature used regularly / now and then / given up / never; searches with no result; activity boards started and finished; suggestions kept; settings and languages chosen), Requests (messages by subject, votes), Bugs (technical problems by day, kind, screen, version, system), Content (pictograms, words, languages), Security (what is shared, retention, the team's actions). Plus a Monday e-mail with the week's figures. To add later: subscriptions and revenue, store figures, costs.

questions.q: Which data can be collected anonymously or in aggregated form?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Everything shown about children's use: sums over at least 5 children of 5 families, consenting families only. Technical problems: stored with no link to anyone. Account counts are the company's own customer statistics.

questions.q: Can we monitor active users, subscriptions and revenue without identifying individuals?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Active users: yes (devices seen in the last 7 and 30 days, counted). Subscriptions and revenue: once billing exists, from RevenueCat or the stores' reports, or a database view of counts and sums, never per child.

questions.q: Can we identify the most frequently used features?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, among consenting families: 30 fixed counter names (16 features, 14 "inside a task" counters) summed per day.

questions.q: Can we identify features that are rarely used or have never been activated?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes: the "given up" and "never" categories of the adoption chart.

questions.q: Can we distinguish between features that are unavailable, undiscovered and intentionally unused?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Only partly. "Unavailable" can be inferred from app version and system, but is not linked to the feature counters. Use counters alone cannot tell "never found it" from "found it and chose not to".

Add "seen" counters (the panel or tip was shown) next to "used" counters, and an optional one-tap question ("useful for us / not for us"), all inside the same fixed, consent-based lists (the database must be updated with the app, as the project rule requires).

questions.q: Can we identify where users experience difficulties or abandon a process?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Partly: searches with no result, activity boards started but not finished, time to create one, suggestions replaced by hand. Abandonment during the set-up is deliberately not measured: it happens before the family has agreed to anything. A lawyer could confirm whether server-side counts with no identifier (profiles created versus first board used) are acceptable.

questions.q: Can we monitor registration, conversion, retention and cancellation rates?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Registrations per week and the path account → child profile → linked device → used this week: yes (Administration page). Retention per person: not shown, by choice. Conversion and cancellation: once billing exists (RevenueCat provides them).

questions.q: Can we identify the reasons for subscription cancellations?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Not yet. Under the plan every cancellation happens in the stores: use the stores' cancellation reports and RevenueCat's cancellation-reason survey, plus an optional question in the app when a family's subscription ends.

questions.q: Can we monitor technical performance by device, operating system and application version?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Problems and devices by system and version: yes. Speed (start-up time, sync time, delay before the voice speaks): not measured; add timing counters in buckets (consent-based, no identifiers).

questions.q: Can we monitor usage and profitability by country?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Professionals' countries are known; families' countries are not collected (no location, by design).
Revenue by country will come from store and payment data; the board's languages and dialect are a usable proxy for usage. Asking the country at sign-up (optional) is a trade-off to decide.

questions.q: Can we identify which features generate the highest infrastructure costs?
questions.label: app

answer.p: AI calls per day: yes (in the back office). Other features: from Supabase's usage and API reports, not from the back office. Until 17 November 2026 the 30-second profile refresh dominated; it now sends only a version number.

questions.q: Can we evaluate the impact of new features and updates?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, roughly: adoption trends week by week and the spread of app versions. To compare before / after a version precisely, add the app version to the daily counters. Avoid A/B tests on the child's board: consistency matters more than optimisation in AAC.

questions.q: Can we generate automated financial and product performance reports?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Product: yes, the Monday e-mail. Financial: RevenueCat, App Store Connect and Play Console send their own reports; Supabase and Anthropic show costs. A monthly one-page summary can be assembled by hand at first.

questions.q: How will analytics data inform future development decisions?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: A quarterly product review: votes and messages (what people ask for), adoption (what they use), problems (what breaks), plus therapists' feedback. Rule already written in the project: know the features, not the families.

questions.q: How can analytics be implemented without collecting private communication content?
questions.label: app

answer.p: As it is done now: fixed lists of counter names shared by the app and the database, whole numbers only, no words, sentences or error messages, sums over at least 5 children of 5 families, consent that is versioned and asked again when the list grows, erasure when the family stops, 180-day retention, nothing from professionals' or the team's accounts.

questions.q: What are the costs associated with storing and processing analytics data?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Negligible: a few hundred bytes per child per day, a few MB a month at 10,000 children, inside the included database size; no third-party analytics fee.

sections.title: Quality assurance and testing
sections.in_short: Automatic testing is strong for a young product (unit, database security, accessibility and browser tests). What is missing is everything that needs real devices and real people: native builds on tablets, offline and sync tests on devices, load tests, payment tests, and usability sessions with AAC users, caregivers and therapists.

questions.q: What testing procedures will be implemented before launch?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Existing: type check; 300 unit tests (grammar, search, permissions, sync merges, consent, analytics, licences, guide wording, colour contrast); 176 database checks including every attack from the security review; a live end-to-end test on a second Supabase project (13 steps, to run again since the back office was added); 204 accessibility scans of 57 screens; browser walkthroughs.
To add: native builds on real tablets, beta testers, offline and sync tests on devices, a load test, usability tests with AAC users, a release checklist.

questions.q: How will the application be tested across different devices and operating systems?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: A small matrix: current and previous iPadOS on a recent and an older iPad; one iPhone; two Android tablets (one low-end, Android 12–16); two Android phones; Chrome, Safari, Edge and Firefox on a computer. Buy 4–6 devices or rent a device cloud.

questions.q: How will offline functionality be tested?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Airplane-mode scenarios on real devices: start offline, speak, edit offline then reconnect (merge), a conflicting change from another device, sign out offline, several days offline, a missing voice, low storage. Merging is already unit-tested; devices are not.

questions.q: How will synchronization between devices be tested?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Two devices editing at once, a use-only tablet, version conflicts, a professional's proposal while a parent edits offline, undo after a merge. Unit and live tests cover part of it; add a device test script.

questions.q: How will data loss prevention and recovery be tested?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: A quarterly restore of the latest backup into a separate project, an export / import round trip, old-profile conversion tests (exist), replacing a device, and checking that account deletion really removes everything.

questions.q: How will payment and subscription systems be tested?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: When billing exists: Apple sandbox and StoreKit testing, Google test tracks and licence testers, RevenueCat sandbox. Scenarios: monthly and yearly purchase, renewal, change between monthly and yearly, refund, grace period, failed payment, the therapist's one-time purchase on a second device, the same subscription on an iPhone and an Android tablet of the family, the linked tablet unlocked, the purchase screen refused without the caregiver code, restore purchases, family sharing, and above all: communication still works after a failed payment.

questions.q: How will security, privacy and accessibility be tested?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Security: the database attack suite, app guard tests, dependency audit, Supabase advisor, a yearly external test. Privacy: tests that nothing is sent without consent (exist). Accessibility: automatic scans, contrast tests, manual screen-reader checks, user tests.

questions.q: How will multilingual functionality be tested?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Existing tests check the guide's button names in three languages, the set-up help, the dialects (12 tests) and the Arabic right-to-left screens. To add: a native-speaker review of each dialect list and of the Arabic menus; the speech therapist's review of the French vocabulary (a review guide already exists); a check that long translations do not overflow.

questions.q: Will AAC users, caregivers and professionals participate in usability testing?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: They should, before launch: so far the app was tried by the owner's circle on an iPad and a review guide was written for a speech therapist. Plan structured sessions with consent forms (parents' consent and the child's assent).

questions.q: What criteria must be met before releasing the application or an update?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Proposal: all automatic checks pass; no open critical or major bug; the core layout test shows no moved word; accessibility scan clean; a 30-minute manual check on one iPad, one Android tablet and one phone; an offline check; database changes applied to staging first; release notes and guide updated in three languages; a rollback plan. If it becomes a medical device: a signed change record.

questions.q: How will bugs be classified and prioritized?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Critical: communication impossible, a wrong word spoken, data loss, privacy leak: fixed at once.
Major: a feature broken with a workaround: next release (1–2 weeks). Minor: cosmetic: backlog.
Security issues also scored by severity. In AAC, wrong speech output is always critical.

questions.q: How will we measure application reliability over time?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Crash-free sessions (needs crash reporting or extending the app's own counters), technical problems per 1,000 child-days (Bugs page), sync success rate, server uptime (a free uptime monitor), time to fix critical bugs.

questions.q: What are the recurring costs associated with quality assurance?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Devices €1,500–€3,000 once; device cloud €0–€200 a month; beta testing free; user testing €3,000–€10,000 a round; testing time about 10–20% of development time; an external tester €300–€500 a day if needed.

sections.title: Legal liability and insurance
sections.in_short: The company will owe users a working, conforming and secure service, and from 9 December 2026 EU law treats software as a product for strict liability. No terms of use or privacy policy exist in the app yet. Liability for injury caused by negligence cannot be excluded, so resilience, clear guidance and insurance matter more than disclaimers.

questions.q: What legal responsibilities does the company have towards AAC users?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Contractual (provide what is described; conformity and security updates under the EU Digital Content Directive); product liability (the new EU directive includes software, from 9 December 2026); data protection (fines and damages); consumer law; accessibility promises; and, if it is a medical device, the manufacturer's duties (vigilance, post-market surveillance). Beyond law, a moral duty of continuity: the app is someone's voice.

questions.q: What are the risks associated with technical failures or loss of user data?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Loss of a personalised vocabulary (months of work), inability to communicate at a critical moment (pain, danger), a breach of children's data: claims, regulatory action, loss of trust. Mitigations: offline design, backups, media sync, exports and prints, testing, insurance, incident plan.

questions.q: What are the risks associated with inaccurate translations, incorrect speech output or other communication errors?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Sources: a mispronounced word, a grammar engine conjugation error, a wrong dialect word, automatic pictogram translations (already flagged "to review"), an inappropriate AI suggestion. Consequence: a message misunderstood (yes / no, pain). Mitigations: native-speaker and therapist validation, the "to review" flags, family recordings that always win over the voice, AI suggestions always reviewed by an adult before use (already the design), a fast correction process, never changing vocabulary silently.

questions.q: What terms and conditions must users accept?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Terms of use (families); terms for professionals (verification, conduct, confidentiality, materials); privacy policy; consent texts (child's data, follow-up, statistics); subscription terms (price, renewal, cancellation, withdrawal); acceptable use; the continuity pledge; the accessibility statement. For a child, the parent accepts. None of these exists in the app yet.

questions.q: What liability limitations are legally permissible?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: With consumers in the EU and UK you cannot exclude liability for death or injury caused by negligence, for gross negligence or fraud, for statutory consumer rights or for product liability; other liability can be capped reasonably. US rules allow more but vary by state. With businesses, caps are negotiated (often 12 months of fees). Add clear statements: not a substitute for a professional assessment; keep a backup way to communicate.

questions.q: Are different contracts required for individual, professional and institutional users?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Yes: consumer terms (with the subscription terms the stores require); professional terms for therapists (their one-time purchase; they may be controllers for their own notes). An institutional agreement only if organisations are ever sold to: not in the plan.

questions.q: Do we need professional liability insurance?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Yes (professional indemnity, "RC Pro" in France): covers errors in the software and in advice; €500–€3,000 a year for a small company; check that software for health and disability is covered.

questions.q: Do we need product liability insurance?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Yes, especially with the new directive covering software, and mandatory in substance for a medical-device manufacturer (MDR art. 10(16) requires financial cover for liability). Often combined with general liability: €1,000–€5,000 a year.

questions.q: Do we need cybersecurity and data breach insurance?
questions.label: decision

questions.q: Does insurance coverage extend to all countries where the application is distributed?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Often not by default: the US and Canada are frequently excluded or cost more; Gulf public contracts may require a local insurer. Check territory and jurisdiction clauses before entering each market.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: What are the annual costs associated with legal advice and insurance?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: First year: legal €8,000–€25,000 (terms, privacy, DPIA, contract templates, medical-device opinion).
Then €3,000–€10,000 a year, plus an external DPO €2,400–€9,600. Insurance €2,500–€12,000 a year (more with US cover). Total after the first year: about €8,000–€30,000 a year.

sections.title: Business continuity and risk management
sections.in_short: Communication itself is resilient (offline boards). The continuity risks are organisational: one person and personal accounts, no backups on the free plan, photos and recordings on single devices, and no written plans. Each has a cheap fix; the table in Part A (A8) lists the main risks with an owner.

questions.q: What are the main technical, financial, legal and operational risks associated with the application?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: Technical: dependence on Supabase; photos and recordings on one device; no staging step; native apps never built or tested on devices; one developer.
Financial: too few paying families; all revenue through two stores (fees, policies, suspension); a therapists' one-time price too low for years of use; AI costs if unlimited.
Legal: medical-device status; health-data hosting (HDS); missing legal documents; unvalidated Arabic content.
Operational: dependence on the founder; support load; manual verification of professionals.

questions.q: What contingency plans should be established?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: One page each: provider outage (offline boards plus a status message), data loss (backups, restore test, exports), developer unavailable (documentation, backup developer), funding gap ("keep it alive" budget), store suspension (installed apps keep working offline; there is no web fallback), regulatory challenge (stop the claims, adjust the intended purpose, start the CE route), breach (incident plan).

questions.q: How frequently are backups performed?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Free plan: never. Supabase Pro: daily, kept 7 days. With point-in-time recovery: continuous. Add an own weekly off-site copy. Devices also hold the latest board.

questions.q: How frequently are backup restoration procedures tested?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Never so far. Every quarter: restore the latest backup into a separate project and check that the app works against it; also after any major database change.

questions.q: What is the maximum acceptable downtime?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Proposal: for speaking on devices, zero, by design; for sync and team features, 4–8 hours, 24 hours at most; for the privacy and support pages, the same day (any static host can serve them).

questions.q: What is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Proposal: 24 hours on the server with daily backups (devices usually hold newer boards), minutes with point-in-time recovery. Photos and recordings are today the unprotected part: fix with media sync.

questions.q: What happens if a hosting provider or third-party service ceases operations?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Supabase is open source: with off-site copies, the data can be restored on self-hosted Supabase or plain PostgreSQL within days; the static pages can move in hours; devices keep working meanwhile. For the other services, see 11.9–11.11.

questions.when: P3 – per new market / at scale

questions.q: What happens if a key developer leaves the project?
questions.label: app

answer.p: See 14.12: today a high risk, reduced by the documentation and tests; reduce it further with company accounts, a second person with access, a backup developer and runbooks.

questions.q: What happens if the company experiences financial difficulties?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Switch to the "keep it alive" budget (about €8,000–€25,000 a year); keep the servers and the continuity pledge first; look for a partner, buyer, foundation or non-profit host; avoid lifetime deals that create obligations nobody pays for.

questions.q: Can the application be transferred or sold to another company?
questions.label: app

answer.p: Yes, if the intellectual property is in the company (assignments), the accounts are in its name, the terms allow transfer with notice, and the apps are moved between developer accounts (both stores allow it). Personal data can follow with notice to users and the same privacy commitments.

questions.q: What happens to existing subscriptions if the company ceases operations?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Under the plan: remove the subscriptions and the therapists' purchase from sale in both stores (renewals then stop), refund unused prepaid periods (yearly subscriptions; the stores handle the refunds), say in the terms what happens to a therapist's one-time purchase, and write the rule in the terms. A liquidator would also be bound by them.

questions.q: How will users recover their communication systems if the application is permanently discontinued?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Through the continuity pledge (15.13): long notice, apps that keep working offline, exports to PDF, the app's file and OBZ (for other AAC apps), and possibly an open-source release.

questions.q: Who is responsible for monitoring and managing each identified risk?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: A risk register with one owner per risk (founder: business and legal; developer: technical; DPO: privacy; clinical lead: content and claims), reviewed every quarter.

sections.title: Pre-launch documentation and responsibilities
sections.in_short: Before real families: backups, two-step sign-in, company-owned accounts, a privacy policy, terms, consent texts, a DPIA draft, provider contracts, and a written decision on medical-device status. Before the paid launch (under the plan: App Store and Google Play only): in-app billing, the store rules of table A5b, store apps tested on devices, a penetration test, an accessibility audit, insurance and tax set-up. Everything else can follow progressively. Part A (A5, A7) gives the costs and order.

questions.q: What technical, financial and legal documentation must be completed before launch?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Technical: architecture overview (mostly done), runbooks (deploy, restore, incident), security policy, access list, test plan and release checklist. Financial: budget, pricing, business plan, tax registrations. Legal: terms, privacy policy, consent texts, DPIA, record of processing, provider contracts, retention schedule, breach procedure, medical-device qualification memo (or technical file), accessibility statement and conformance report, IP assignments, trademark filings, insurance.

questions.q: Which authorizations, licences and certifications must be obtained?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Company registration, D-U-N-S number, developer accounts, VAT registration (OSS). For the device question: either a memo concluding it is not a medical device, or CE class I with EUDAMED registration and a PRRC. Country-specific: Lebanon's declaration of processing, the UK ICO fee, SFDA if a device in Saudi Arabia. No ISO or SOC 2 certification is needed for a consumer launch.

questions.q: Which independent audits must be conducted?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Before selling: a penetration test, an accessibility audit and a legal review of the privacy documents (in practice required), plus native-speaker content reviews. Later: SOC 2 or ISO 27001 if institutions require it.

questions.q: Which policies and contractual agreements must be prepared?
questions.label: expert

answer.p: Privacy policy; a storage notice for the static pages (only necessary storage is used, so no consent banner should be needed: confirm); terms for families and for professionals; subscription terms; acceptable use; institutional agreement, DPA and SLA; provider DPAs; IP assignments; contractor agreements (confidentiality, IP); information security policy; incident response; retention schedule; continuity pledge; accessibility statement.

questions.q: Who is responsible for each area of compliance?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Founder: accountable for everything. Lawyer / DPO: privacy documents and DPIA. Regulatory consultant: medical-device status. Accountant: tax. Developer: technical documentation and security. Clinical lead: content validation and claims. Accessibility auditor: conformance report.

questions.q: Which requirements must be fulfilled before launch and which can be addressed progressively?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Before real families (P0): Supabase Pro and backups; two-step sign-in on every admin account; company-owned accounts; privacy policy, terms and consent texts; DPIA draft; provider contracts; medical-device decision and claims wording; a proper e-mail service; a staging step; pasting the updated reset e-mail template. (Done on 17 November 2026: the light 30-second check and "Forgot the code?".)

Before the paid launch (P1), required by the plan: in-app billing that never blocks communication (subscriptions, the therapists' one-time purchase, the server-side entitlement for every family device, "Restore purchases", the purchase screen behind the caregiver code); store accounts, privacy forms and the other rules of table A5b; device tests. Advised or chosen: media sync; penetration test; accessibility audit; insurance; VAT; trademark filing; native-speaker reviews.
Progressively (P2–P3): switch and eye-gaze access, OBZ export, snapshots, organisation accounts, SOC 2, new countries.

questions.q: What are the estimated costs and deadlines associated with each requirement?
questions.label: estimate

answer.p: See Part A, table A5 (one-off budget by item and phase) and table A7 (the order of work). As a guide: P0 in 4–8 weeks and €12,500–€42,000 if you hire a developer (€10,500–€37,000 in cash if you build it yourself); P1 in a further 2–4 months and €35,000–€105,000 hired (about €17,000–€64,000 in cash built yourself). Built yourself, the development rows cost your time, the stores' fees and test devices only.

questions.q: Who will be responsible for maintaining compliance after launch?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: The founder, with the external DPO for privacy and a compliance calendar that names an owner per area (tax dates, yearly audits, policy reviews, store deadlines, OS cycles).

questions.q: How frequently should technical, financial, security and regulatory assessments be updated?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: Technical and security: every quarter. Financial: key figures monthly, budget yearly. Regulatory: yearly, and before each new country or any feature touching health claims or children's data. This document: every 6 months.

questions.q: What criteria must be met before launching the application in a new country?
questions.label: decision

answer.p: A go / no-go list: privacy law checked (consent age, transfers, localisation); medical-device status there; tax registration; payment methods; store availability and prices; vocabulary and dialect validated by a local speech therapist or native speaker; a device voice exists for the language; support in the language; trademark filed; legal documents translated; accessibility rules for public buyers; a local partner if selling to institutions.

chapters.title: Appendix E · My answers in our conversation

blocks.p: The summaries I gave you in our conversation, gathered here so that every answer is in this one document. Where something has changed since, the status of today is written in bold.

blocks.h2: E1 · Summary of the assessment

bullets: The child can always speak. The board runs on the tablet, works without internet, and words never move. That is the right foundation.
Servers are cheap. About US$40 a month up to roughly 1,000 active children, then 1–4 US cents per child per month. The real costs are people, compliance, and the AI helper if you switch it on.

One habit drove the server bill as you grow: every open board downloaded the child's whole profile every 30 seconds. Fixed on 17 November 2026 (pull request #4): only a version number travels now; servers for 100,000 children fall from about $2,860 to about $875 a month.
There are no backups today. The free server plan keeps none. Moving to the US$25/month plan before real families use the app gives daily backups.
Photos and recordings exist only on the device that made them. A lost tablet loses them. This is the main risk of losing a family's data.

The biggest legal question is whether the app is a medical device. EU law covers software that "compensates for a disability", so the app is probably a low-risk (class I) medical device unless it is presented differently. Get a written opinion before any marketing.
Legal documents are missing. The app has no privacy policy or terms of use yet; the law and both app stores require them.

A child's profile should be treated as health data. That means explicit parental consent, an impact assessment and probably a data protection officer. In France it may also mean using a certified health-data host: a question for your lawyer.
Everything depends on one person. The code and the service accounts look like personal accounts. They should move to the company, with a backup developer named.
There was no "forgot the caregiver code" option, so a family that forgot its code was locked out. Fixed on 17 November 2026 (pull request #5): see E2.

blocks.h3: What I could and could not check

bullets: I read the application's code, database rules, tests and documentation; I measured a new child's profile (12 KB) and checked the licences of all 523 code libraries the app depends on: all of them allow commercial use.
Prices come from public price lists and news of November 2026. Some came only from secondary summaries that did not agree with each other: re-check them before committing money.
The repository does not show which region the server was created in: you can see it in Supabase under Project Settings → General.
Questions marked "Needs an expert" are a guide to what to ask a lawyer, accountant, regulatory consultant or auditor, not advice to rely on.

blocks.h2: E2 · The two fixes made in the app

blocks.p: 1. Boards no longer download the whole profile every 30 seconds. While I was building this, the separate session you started from the suggested task finished the same fix and merged it first (pull request #4). I kept its version, because it also keeps a change made on the board while a newer profile is downloading, and dropped my copy. Each check now sends only a version number, which removes about 99% of the server traffic. No database change was needed.

2. "Forgot the code?" for the caregiver code (pull request #5). Before, a family that forgot its code was locked out, because the setting that changes it is itself behind the code. Now there is a link under the keypad:

bullets: The app e-mails a code to the parent's account (or texts it, for a phone account). The parent types it in, then chooses a new caregiver code. The account password does not change.
A therapist can reset her own code the same way.
On a linked tablet, which has no e-mail, the screen says to do it from a parent's phone or computer.
It is in French, English and Arabic, and the in-app guide mentions it.
All 288 automatic tests passed at the time (300 today on the main branch), and the accessibility suite found no problem on any of its 204 screen checks.
On 18 November, another session extended it (pull request #6): the parent can also prove it with the account's password; Google and Apple accounts use the e-mailed code.

A walk through the whole flow in a browser at computer size, phone size and with Arabic menus: a code was chosen, "Forgot the code?" was used, a wrong code was refused, the right one worked, a new code was chosen, and the old code stopped working. No accessibility problem on the new screens.
Both changes are merged into the branch the website publishes from; Cloudflare rebuilds the site by itself (I could not open the live site from my environment to watch it finish).

blocks.h2: E3 · Are all these costs obligatory? (18 November 2026)

blocks.p: Plan set on 18 November 2026: App Store and Google Play only; families pay monthly or yearly, therapists pay once. Under that plan, no, not all costs are obligatory. Table A4 has a Needed? column and a minimum:

bullets: Minimum under the plan: about $35 a month up to 1,000 active children (Supabase Pro for its backups, the Apple program and a domain), about $60 at 10,000 and about $750 at 100,000, mostly sign-in accounts above the included 100,000. Expo's $19 a month is added when its free builds are not enough; Google Play's $25 is paid once.
Choices, not obligations: point-in-time recovery (Pro already keeps a daily backup for 7 days) and the off-site copy (advised, cheap).

The stores' fee is a cost of the plan: 15% of each sale without VAT (Apple's Small Business Program, once enrolled; Google Play subscriptions), 30% otherwise. At the report's example prices: €1.25 a month per €9.99 monthly subscription, €10.00 a year per €79.99 yearly one. The therapists' price is not set: the company keeps about 0.70 × that price (France). The stores collect VAT.

The AI helper is optional and switched off today (no AI button shows in the app). If you switch it on, Claude Haiku 5.5 costs about 40 times less than Claude Opus 5.5; test the quality first, Arabic first.

Legal duties: the GDPR documents (privacy notice, terms, records of processing) and very likely an impact assessment (DPIA), because the app holds children's data; a data protection officer may be required if the data counts as health data processed at large scale (an external part-time one is usual). An accountant follows from running a company. Insurance, support and maintenance are advised business needs, not legal duties.

Answer 1.1 now splits the launch budget three ways: required by law (legal documents and DPIA, about €7,000–€25,000), the WORK required by the plan (native builds, store set-up, in-app billing with the server entitlement, Sign in with Apple, the stores' privacy forms: €14,000–€34,000 only if you hire a developer; built yourself, Apple's US$99 a year, Google Play's US$25 once, test devices if needed, and your time), advised (audits, insurance, content review). The whole launch budget is €48,000–€147,000 hired, or about €28,000–€101,000 in cash built yourself (table A5). The €120,000–€350,000 figure is not money to pay: it is what an agency would charge to rebuild what exists.
CE marking is not automatic: it depends on how the app's purpose is described; ask a regulatory specialist before spending €25,000–€80,000.

Native apps only (decided 18 November 2026): the web app is not offered; the privacy and support pages stay online as static pages. The launch plan (the chapter after Part A) lists everything still to do.

Launch plan added (18 November 2026): one list of everything still to do until the app is on both stores, by phase, with who, cost, time, what each item waits for and its status, the owner's decisions and a timeline with the critical path.
